The newly open source cuSpa accelerates cell polygon calculations, enabling developers to generate massive spatial graphs for next-generation patient and cancer models at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, with a 900x speedup compared with using CPUs.

# CUDA at 20: How the Platform Transformed Scientific Computing

 Over two decades, CUDA, the platform that turned GPUs into the engine of modern science, has advanced Nobel Prize-winning research and more.

November 16, 2026 by[Brett Murray](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/author/bmurray/ "Posts by Brett Murray")

 Share

Share This Article

This week at SC26, NVIDIA is marking two decades of [CUDA](https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda) by honoring the researchers, developers and engineers who helped make GPU computing a foundation for modern science and AI.

CUDA’s 20th anniversary presents an occasion to reflect across computing eras, from the people who wrote the very first CUDA programs to the AI developers building on their work today.

At the platform’s core is this developer community whose experiments, tools and persistence expanded what accelerated computing could do.

## **From SC06 to SC26**

NVIDIA [announced CUDA in November 2006](https://web.archive.org/web/20220706095459/https://www.clustermonkey.net/Conference-Reports/sc06-jeffs-blog-day-1-sunday/Print.html) and brought it to the scientific community at SC06, giving scientists and developers a familiar, high-level programming model for using GPUs. It fundamentally extended accelerated computing beyond graphics use cases to accelerate demanding applications for science, simulation and more.

In the two decades since, developers have used CUDA to advance [Nobel Prize-winning AI research](https://www.kva.se/en/news/the-nobel-prize-in-chemistry-2024/), accelerate [scientific applications on supercomputers](https://docs.nersc.gov/performance/readiness/) and support [visual effects in Oscar-winning films](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-quadro-powers-all-five-academy-award-nominees-for-best-visual-effects).

Today, [more than 11 million developers](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/gtc-2026-news/#cuda) build on CUDA across the computing stack.

## **Honoring the Architects of Progress**

Now, at SC26, NVIDIA is looking back at some of the CUDA luminaries who’ve spearheaded breakthroughs in science and AI:

At the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, biophysicist Klaus Schulten’s team helped connect GPU computing with molecular biology through [Nanoscale Molecular Dynamics and Visual Molecular Dynamics](https://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/academia/whitepapers/Achievement2014_UIUC.pdf), tools for molecular simulation and visualization. In 2013, researchers at Illinois, the University of Pittsburgh and Vanderbilt University used CUDA-accelerated tools to help resolve the HIV capsid’s atomic structure. They combined experiments with simulations on [Blue Waters](https://www.ks.uiuc.edu/Highlights/?highlight=2013-06&section=2013), one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers at the time.

In a critical breakthrough in AI, University of Toronto researchers Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton used CUDA to [train AlexNet](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2012/file/c399862d3b9d6b76c8436e924a68c45b-Paper.pdf) on just two NVIDIA GPUs. Their image-recognition system [won the 2012 ImageNet competition](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2012/file/c399862d3b9d6b76c8436e924a68c45b-Paper.pdf), helping demonstrate the potential of GPU computing for deep learning.

That connection between computing and scientific discovery is seen with AlphaFold, which predicts protein structures. Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for protein structure prediction. Their team’s [publicly released AlphaFold 2 software](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold)[uses CUDA for GPU execution](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/blob/main/docker/Dockerfile).

These are just a few of many examples that show how one generation’s work creates opportunities for the next. With 1,000+ NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, developers are now reshaping industries and giving machines the power to see, learn and reason — from discovering new medicines and designing next-generation factories to advancing autonomous vehicles, modeling financial markets and unlocking quantum computing — and more.

# NVIDIA Announces Rubin HPC — A New GPU to Accelerate Agents for Science, Engineering and Analytics

 A record leap in CUDA cores with accelerated data movement shorten time to results for science and engineering workloads.

November 16, 2026 by[Dan Ernst](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/author/dernst/ "Posts by Dan Ernst")

 Share

Share This Article

Announced today at SC26, NVIDIA Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the [NVIDIA Vera Rubin](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/technologies/rubin/) platform designed to accelerate simulation and data processing for science, engineering and analytics workflows.

As agents help scientists and engineers explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs, they rely on simulations to test those ideas and guide their next steps. Rubin HPC will accelerate those simulations, shortening the path from exploration to scientific discovery and industrial design.

The Rubin HPC GPU features a record number of CUDA cores — more than 50,000 on a single GPU — as well as a sparse data acceleration capability that keeps those cores fed with data, and accelerates GPU-to-GPU connectivity with seventh-generation [NVIDIA NVLink](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/nvlink/) interconnect technology.

Scientists and engineers rely on simulation to understand complex systems before committing to experiments or physical prototypes. Working with agents, these teams can explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs. This increases demand for the GPU-accelerated simulations needed to evaluate those ideas and guide next steps.

“For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery,” said Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer.”

## **Turning Faster Computation Into Faster Discovery**

Across climate models, engineering simulations, genomic analysis and financial risk, scientific computing workloads take a similar shape: an application reaches into an immense dataset, gathers a handful of scattered values, calculates a result and repeats this on an enormous scale.

To help address the challenge, Rubin HPC will offer a balanced design, scaling data movement and compute together rather than increasing compute alone.

That balance is what optimizes Rubin HPC for scientific computing. It keeps the GPU’s record number of CUDA cores supplied with data, so they spend their time computing rather than waiting. This accelerates recurring patterns of every simulation workload — from sparse matrix operations to stencil computations to sorting and reductions.

These patterns are prevalent across data analytics, science and engineering workloads, which is why a purpose-built GPU delivering the broadest acceleration can help unlock cross-industry breakthroughs.

[NVIDIA CUDA-X](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/technologies/cuda-x/) libraries offer a growing set of optimized implementations of complex algorithms for agents to use, including those most relevant to simulation and analytics. Used together with Rubin HPC, the libraries can give agents the fastest glide path to reasoning outcomes.

And faster agent-invoked simulations mean faster feedback — shortening the loop of hypothesis, simulation and refinement, so researchers and engineers can choose next steps sooner and point lab work at the most promising candidates.

_Rubin HPC is expected to be available in 2028._

Nvidia interim CEO and longtime CFO Colette Kress is about to have one of the biggest days of her career on Tuesday when the company reports its third-quarter results.
For the first time, Kress will be running through the numbers and sharing guidance without Nvidia’s charismatic but now-disgraced founder Jensen Huang.
Huang was
forced to resign last week
after he admitted to having an affair with an exec of a customer, Alice Huang, a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, and he was accused of having two more affairs with Nvidia employees.
Now, the company is facing questions about its restricted chips allegedly being smuggled into China, especially by Huang’s mistress’ company. Nvidia promised to conduct an internal investigation. Meanwhile, Huang was
commanded to answer questions to Congress
in a closed-door joint session with three Republican-led committees. Plus, top Democrats
have also vowed to investigate the company.
Given the turmoil Nvidia is in, there are a number of questions that Kress should answer.
Huang’s role now and going forward.
Huang ran Nvidia with an iron fist, having some 60 direct reports and his fingers in everything. No one knows the company better than him.
An internet petition signed by 180,000
and growing is calling for the board to reinstate him. Huang may also have been mounting an attempt to return,
Financial Times
reported. However,
CNBC is
reporting, citing unnamed sources, that the company is not in talks to reinstate Huang.
So, we’ll be looking for language from the interim CEO about Huang’s ongoing involvement with the company, its search for a new CEO, and any talks to bring him back.
China and Singapore.
As Huang
vehemently argued
in favor of easing export restrictions for Nvidia chips to China, Huang said that he’s seen no evidence that its powerful
semiconductors were being diverted from legit buyers to China.
But in October 2025,
The New York Times
reported that the U.S. was investigating Huang’s mistress’ company, Megaspeed, over allegations it was doing just that. Nvidia at the time
vouched to CNBC
that Megaspeed was legally using the chips for its cloud. However, Nvidia recently told
The Wall Street Journal
that it had voluntarily blocked Megaspeed from receiving more chips way back in June 2025.
Last year, Nvidia said that Singapore, the region where Megaspeed is located, was one of its fastest-growing, accounting
for 22% of its total revenue
for its second quarter of that year. After the investigation into Megaspeed came to light, Nvidia changed how it reported revenue. It now reports based on a company’s headquarters, instead of its shipping address. That completely hid sales to Singapore and Megaspeed’s impact.
So we’re listening to what Kress says about the future of sales to the China region and the cloud business in Singapore that was once 20% of sales. We’re especially listening for what she says about Nvidia keeping track of where its restricted chips wind up.
China sales policy.
Huang’s argument was, essentially, that the U.S. can’t stop China from developing advanced AI models, so the West is better off selling them less powerful Nvidia chips and keeping them dependent, he said on the
Dwarkesh Podcast
last summer. Notably, that’s a position that would make Nvidia a lot of money.
The China hawks counter that selling an adversary any powerful chips at all will help them, and U.S. companies shouldn’t do that. So we’re listening for any indications that Kress is reversing Nvidia’s goals with China.
Bankrolling the AI build-out.
The expectation is that Kress, the CFO who reportedly had unsuccessfully tried to
push back against Huang’s extreme AI dealmaking,
will be conservative on such deals going forward. We’ll be listening for what she says about the impacts of existing deals on the books. (Will she subtly try to throw Huang under the bus for
those controversial deals
?) We’ll also be listening for her future plans.
Governance.
With the ousting of Huang
and more fallout sure still to come
, has the board learned its lesson about too much power in the hands of one person? We’ll be listening for information about how Nvidia might restructure itself.

articles.title: California state AG sues OpenAI over rogue agent incidents
articles.summary: The California lawsuit represents one of the first attempts to hold an AI lab legally accountable for a rogue agent incident.
articles.content:
OpenAI is facing
a new lawsuit from the California Attorney General’s office
, alleging that the company’s training practices and lax security pose an ongoing danger to the public.
At the center of the case is
the July 2026 Hugging Face compromise
, in which a pre-release model within OpenAI compromised both companies’ security systems to complete a training benchmark. In
its official report on the incident
, OpenAI called it “an outlier scenario involving a rare and unexpected confluence of events.”
The California lawsuit represents one of the first attempts by a government regulator to hold an AI lab legally accountable for a rogue agent incident, with significant implications for both OpenAI’s competitors and its clients.
The complaint
centers on the Hugging Face incident, but also cites similar incidents involving
RubyGems
,
DseWiki
,
the Wikimedia Foundation
, and
Australian government websites
as evidence that the underlying behavior is ongoing.
The complaint also alleges that dozens of similar incidents have occurred without public disclosure.
“OpenAI has recently sent notices to dozens of additional third parties whose websites or internal systems have been infiltrated by OpenAI agents,” the complaint reads. “In some cases, OpenAI agents were able to access sensitive personally identifiable information, such as employee records containing names, birth dates, addresses, and more. The vast majority of these incidents have not been disclosed or discussed publicly by either OpenAI or by the affected third parties.”
The central allegation is that OpenAI’s ongoing testing practices constitute a public nuisance because the lack of safety controls present an ongoing risk to the public. A secondary claim alleges unfair competition stemming from the marketing of an unsafe product. If the lawsuit succeeds, OpenAI could face an injunction “to abate the ongoing public nuisance,” leaving broad discretion in the hands of the court.
It’s the first regulatory case targeting OpenAI specifically over rogue agent incidents, although public endangerment claims have been considered by other states. In June, the Florida attorney general sued the company over
allegedly harmful effects on users
, particularly children and teenagers. In August, the Alabama attorney general
launched a probe
into deceptive practices related to the breach, but no case has been filed.
In a statement to the press, California Attorney General Rob Bonta presented the case as an effort to maintain public safety in the face of a powerful new technology.
“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-word cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society. The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it,” Bonta said in the statement. “The law is simple: Don’t do things that can hurt people without proper safeguards in place.”
In a statement, OpenAI emphasized the company’s extensive effort to investigate the Hugging Face incident and improve its systems in the aftermath.
“This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” OpenAI said. “We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”

articles.title: Trump says ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy did not threaten national security
articles.summary: Trump contradicted his own government's intelligence officials, who reportedly concluded that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy.
articles.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump
told reporters on Monday
that he does not believe the country’s national security was put at risk as a result of former Nvidia CEO
Jensen Huang’s affair
with an alleged Chinese spy.
“It was not put at risk,” Trump said when asked by reporters in light of his own friendship with Huang. “Our country is now stronger than ever before. And you know, China plays games with us, and we play games with China.”
Trump went on to contradict
previous findings
from U.S. officials by doubting that Huang’s paramour, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy.
“He probably shouldn’t have been doing on a personal basis what he did … That’s a different story,” Trump added. “But nobody’s proven that she’s a spy. She may not be a spy.”
Last year, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly oversaw the production of an internal memo, circulated among top policymakers, which warned that Alice Huang was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. Trump was reportedly
briefed
about these intelligence findings at least twice, including once in May aboard Air Force One, shortly before the former Nvidia CEO joined him on a trip to China. But Trump has maintained that he was not aware of these claims.
The U.S. regulates the exports of Nvidia’s top chips to China as a way of maintaining a competitive advantage. But prior to news of Huang’s affair publicly emerging, both the U.S. and Singaporean governments had been
investigating
Megaspeed for illegally smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Huang has since stepped down from the role he has had for 33 years at Nvidia after more reporting revealed that he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees, at least one of whom was a direct report.
Given Huang’s importance to Nvidia, some prominent figures in the industry — including Elon Musk, Y Combinator president and CEO Garry Tan, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney —
have signed a public letter
calling for Nvidia to reinstate Huang.
“A lot of people are asking Jensen — they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea,” Trump said. Referring to the former Apple chief executive, Trump added: “I
recommended
Tim Cook.”

articles.title: Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: The industry will be ‘fine’
articles.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman acknowledged the special role Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has played in the AI boom, but ultimately thinks the industry will be “fine” without him at the helm.
articles.content:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says the AI industry will be “fine” without Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the helm, even as he acknowledged the special role Huang has played in the AI boom.
Huang resigned
last week from Nvidia after admitting to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Altman made his first public comments about Huang’s departure on Monday at
Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World
event, where he also discussed topics ranging from data center pushback to recursive self-improvement.
Numerous executives and members of the AI industry have argued for Nvidia to reinstate Huang, including Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney, who were among the signatories in a
public letter.
Many fear that Huang’s departure may cause Nvidia to rethink the enormous financial risks it has taken that have fueled the AI boom.
Huang is also reportedly setting up a
“war room”
of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return.
When asked whether he thought Huang should return to the company, Altman said: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.”
He expressed empathy for Huang’s situation, citing his own
ousting from OpenAI
in 2023 after board members accused him of withholding information.
“It’s hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen and the company he has built,” Altman said, adding that he sees Huang as a hero, and that “heroes have flaws.”
OpenAI and Nvidia have had a close relationship for the last decade, one that has evolved from a simple chip supplier-customer relationship into a potentially circular financing arrangement, in which Nvidia’s money helps fund purchases of its own chips. Most recently, Nvidia agreed to provide a guarantee of up to $105 billion backing OpenAI’s Ohio data center project. That’s just one of many such circular deals Nvidia has made to bankroll the AI boom while fueling demand for its own chips.
Altman said he’s not worried that the Bank of Nvidia will dry up.
“Nvidia is, like, a behemoth of a company,” he said. “I think people still trust their guarantees very much.”
Altman acknowledged the “ambition” Huang brought to the industry, the scale of which “has been quite important.” But he didn’t go so far as to agree with the many who worry about ripple effects from Huang’s departure.
“I think there’s so much demand, and it’s so clear that AI is real, and people want to use it, and the revenues and demand are growing so strongly that I think the industry will be fine,” Altman said. “But again, I think Jensen has played this extremely special and valuable role as someone to really drive things forward with great ambition.”

articles.title: FBI says Artex AI open source hacking tool used to breach networks in ‘under three hours’
articles.summary: The FBI says that the open source hacking tool was used in cyberattacks targeting a U.S. IT giant and the South Korean financial industry.
articles.content:
The FBI is warning that hackers are relying on autonomous AI hacking tools to launch cyberattacks across the U.S. and globally. The campaigns include a widespread hack of customers of American IT company ConnectWise and across South Korea’s financial industry.
In its
latest flash cybersecurity advisory
, the FBI says hackers have targeted several industries in recent months, including financial services, government, tech, defense, phone and internet companies, and law firms, using open source tools like Artex to carry out autonomous-driven cyberattacks.
Artex is one of several open source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network’s defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be “noisy,” meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company’s defensive alerts. But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that make it far more difficult for human defenders to keep up.
In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise “in under three hours.”
The FBI’s warning comes as AI-powered hacks are escalating, particularly by finding easy-to-find security flaws and breaking into companies with relative ease.
Oftentimes, Artex will rely on rapidly scanning a victim’s network to look for signs of weakness, and then exploit simple security bugs, such as weak protections and exposed or stolen passwords to gain a foothold. From there, Artex allows the hacker to spread across the network for databases, mailboxes, and other sensitive information.
The FBI’s advisory noted that Artex has been used in several cyberattacks since the tool’s first public debut in July. Artex was used to hack a number of South Korean financial institutions, blamed in large part on weak cybersecurity defenses and lacking protections, such as multi-factor authentication. The attacks allowed hackers to
steal the personal data
of at least 68,000 people.
The FBI confirmed
earlier findings from Microsoft
that hackers also used Artex to break into IT management giant ConnectWise and gain access to the Microsoft 365 cloud environments of
at least 2,250
of its customers.
The hackers, who Microsoft says are likely Chinese, used the tool to steal data from affected ConnectWise customers.
A spokesperson for ConnectWise did not respond to a request for comment about the FBI’s claim.
Cybersecurity company Barracuda
also disclosed
that it was breached as part of an Artex-linked attack by financially motivated criminals, in which the tool found an exposed credential belonging to a third-party service that Barracuda had not revoked when it ended work with the vendor. That access allowed the hackers to access stores of credentials used by Barracuda to collect data from its customers’ systems. Barracuda said it couldn’t rule out access, as its logs were not detailed enough, and chose to “assume the worst” and changed all of its customer credentials.
“Defenders who rely on spotting malicious activity and then responding to it will often arrive after the attacker has finished,” wrote Barracuda’s chief information security officer, Arve Kjoelen.
A spokesperson for Barracuda told TechCrunch that the company “directly notified and advised a minority of XDR customers to revoke and recreate integration credentials,” but did not specify how many customers.
After Artex was used in cyberattacks, the tool’s developer made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks. But the FBI says the previous open source version continues to circulate and remains “widely accessible” for use in cyberattacks.
It’s not only companies and targeted victims that have been compromised as a result of weakened security exploited by AI tools; the tools themselves have been exposed as well, potentially allowing outsiders to access powerful hacking capabilities. Last week, researchers
found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online
, which had been placed on the internet without a password, likely by mistake or misconfiguration — including the Artex system that was used to target South Korea.

articles.title: Jordan Belfort’s new AI voice startup, Tone, wants to sell like the ‘Wolf of Wall Street’
articles.summary: Belfort claims his AI sales voice can already close deals almost as well as the best human salespeople, and he thinks it will catch up in a year.
articles.content:
Years ago, as questions mounted about WeWork’s soaring valuation, I sat down with co-founder Adam Neumann. We were negotiating a stage interview, and he asked to meet me twice in the weeks leading up to it, once at a WeWork in San Francisco and again at his office in New York.
I knew full well that the numbers that SoftBank in particular had assigned to WeWork
made little sense
, but I came away understanding why investors wanted to throw in their lot with him.
It’s similarly easy to understand why people are enchanted by Jordan Belfort, the self-proclaimed “Wolf of Wall Street.” Belfort famously pleaded guilty in 1999 to securities fraud and money laundering tied to Stratton Oakmont, the Long Island brokerage where salespeople pushed penny stocks in pump-and-dump schemes while Belfort acquired a Southampton mansion, a 167-foot yacht, and at least one helicopter. (He destroyed the latter two while high on quaaludes and cocaine, as depicted in Martin Scorsese’s famous adaptation of Belfort’s autobiography, “The Wolf of Wall Street.”)
You might think someone who spent 22 months in prison and was ordered to pay $110.4 million in restitution to 1,513 victims wouldn’t get another shake. The victims ultimately received “far less” than they were owed, TMZ
reported in July
, noting that Belfort completed his court-ordered restitution obligations in late April of this year.
But Belfort, whose energy has a galvanizing quality, keeps resurfacing, including in recent years as a Miami-based sales consultant and one-time host of crypto workshops at his Miami Beach home. (A New York Times reporter attended a
weekend workshop
several years ago where the price of admission was one bitcoin or its equivalent value at the time of $40,000.)
Now he is moving into the intersection of what he knows best — sales — and the hottest trend on the planet, AI, building out a voice-based AI platform. The secret sauce is that it imbues its voices with the kind of tonality that wins deals, he says, for example, by phrasing declarative statements as questions (which “builds engagement”) and even whispering at times (which “implies scarcity of information”).
Belfort says the platform, called
Tone
, is already being used by companies that have more sales leads than their human teams can handle. Now, in a move that could also help expand its training data, Tone is launching a self-service platform for content creators and authors who want to turn their books into “expressive AI-generated narration.” Users can select from Tone’s AI voices or, as a voice-cloning feature rolls out, create a clone of their own voice.
It’s easy to argue the market is already saturated with AI voice startups and technologies, and Tone comes with added risk: Belfort’s co-founder in the business is longtime investor Shervin Pishevar, who has a
controversial past
of his own. We also can’t independently verify that the technology works as described (neither co-founder is an engineer).
But if my time with Neumann taught me anything, it’s that doubts about the numbers rarely get in the way of a good pitch. When Belfort looks for investors to back him in this new venture, finding believers won’t be too hard.
Here is part of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.
What have you built?
It’s a very unique way of going about building a voice, and it stems from a system of influence and persuasion I’ve been teaching since the late 1980s. It’s not just what you say, but how you say it. When you’re not in person, body language collapses into tonality. There are about 15 very powerful tonalities that people use all the time. The phrase I invented for this was “goal-oriented communication.” If I’m trying to be perceived as an expert, I apply tonality strategically.
Is this effectively trained on you?
It started that way. As a non-engineer, I went to first principles: How would I teach a human to do this? One tonality at a time. I have 30 years of super high-quality data , and I started teaching the model. It was a breakthrough moment, because it not only sounded exactly like me, it had nailed the tonality. Then I taught it a second one, and then how to link them. The key to all of this is data. Even the littlest bit of corrupt data dramatically negates the progress you’ve made.
How did you and Shervin Pishevar come together?
Shervin and I have been personal friends for a long time, and we were out for dinner one night. I had been pitched by an AI company that said it had an AI that could do selling. I listened to it. It was awful. But it put the idea in my head. I thought I was just going to teach models how to sell, but I couldn’t find a voice that was good enough. Necessity is the mother of invention, so we built our own.
Who are your customers, and how do they use it?
We have law firms and health insurance companies. We do a lot in polling and automobiles. It will take you through an entire health insurance sale. It asks qualifying questions, like what type of insurance you want, your budget, your ages. Then it chooses a plan and explains the features and benefits. Our latency is like 600 milliseconds. If the payment is too high, it’ll say it can bring the payment down and explain how to raise your deductible. If you don’t like the plan, it swaps you to a different one. It does literally the whole entire sale.
How does the AI handle a sales call that goes off script?
It never says, “That’s a great question,” unless it really is. I hate that. It’s so ingratiating. In any sale there’s a happy path, how we’d want the perfect conversation to go, and every last word can be mapped out. But people have questions and concerns, and they take you off the straight line. So the trick is a model that can carry that perfect conversation, handle anything thrown at it, answer elegantly and return to the straight line, without breaking rapport and without hallucinating — or, as a salesperson, lying. We’ve trained the model to do that.
Have you generated any revenue from Tone yet? Have you raised funding for it?
Revenue, probably about a million bucks — $700,000, maybe. We’ve raised friends and family and seed, about $10 million.
I want to address the elephant in the room. You have a fraud conviction. Pishevar has faced misconduct allegations that he
denies
. Why should a bank or a hospital or a consumer brand trust this product coming from the two of you?
All I can say for myself is that I did make mistakes. It was a very, very long time ago, and I’ve spent the last 20-plus years teaching people all over the world. I’ve been hired by companies all over the world to teach sales and persuasion. If some companies don’t want to work with us, that’s their decision. But I think there would be more than enough that would see the value of what we created.
What close rate does Tone have versus a typical sales force?
I still don’t think it’s quite as good as a top producer. A top producer in the field would outdo it call for call. I think that will change in the next six months to a year. To make a model respond this quickly, you’re not using frontier models. We’re using our own very small, very light models, so they don’t have quite as much intelligence. I think it will significantly outperform a mediocre closer.
Where is it used most effectively? Low-dollar sales opportunities?
I’d think the more money someone is spending, the more human contact they’d demand.
I don’t think it’s about replacing humans. What I see most with customers is that they simply don’t have the human capital available. They could get a lot more leads than they have people to call, or they need coverage at different times of day or in different languages. I think there’s always going to be a need for great human salespeople. I really believe that.
You’re competing with ElevenLabs and Cartesia and a lot of other voice AI companies. Tone is your edge?
I don’t think sounding human is really what this is about. They’ll all sound human in six months or a year. It’s the application of tonality that makes us different: the intelligence behind when it chooses a certain tonality. We have a patent on it. ElevenLabs is a great company, and Cartesia as well, but those voices didn’t work for us.
The FCC ruled in 2024 that AI voices fall under robocall rules under the
Telephone Consumer Protection Act
. How does outbound sales calling work?
We only call opt-in. You’re not going to use AI to cold-call people. We would not allow that. You’d get sued by every TCPA lawyer in the world. It’s either opted-in leads or existing customers. The exception is polling, where there’s an exemption that lets you call private homes without opt-in.
How do you verify consent and prevent impersonation in voice cloning?
We could launch the cloning tomorrow. We didn’t. If you create a clone in our system, you speak into the computer, so we know who is creating it, and that person signs a consent. If someone wants to upload audio, which we don’t recommend, you’d have to match a live voiceprint in real time.
Who created the technology? You’re not an engineer, and Pishevar isn’t, either. I saw a name on the
patent
, Jordan Anthony Metzner.
No. Our VP of engineering is Ben Sussman. He’s a brilliant engineer. I’m the judge and the jury and the executioner of what sounds perfect. I’ll prototype something in the most obscene way, and my engineers rebuild it from scratch.
Do you charge per minute, or based on the outcomes customers see?
A combination. For streaming, it’s per minute. The content platform will be monthly subscriptions. And we have some clients where the bulk of our money is made through success.
Is this an independent company or something that belongs inside a larger AI company?
If the right offer came up, and it was substantial enough, and I thought it made sense, who wouldn’t entertain a conversation? But right now my plan is to raise a significant amount. I don’t think we need to own data centers, but we need enough reserve compute. I wouldn’t think I’d be selling it anytime soon, but who knows what the future brings.
Paramount+ released a
documentary
about you this summer. Did you watch it?
I didn’t. Believe it or not, I don’t watch or read anything about me, good or bad. I never read a comment. When you’re well-known, you have to live by who you are inside. I go by my own internal compass.

articles.title: OpenAI will embed safety researchers to investigate AI subversion
articles.summary: OpenAI will embed six Apollo Research evaluators to investigate whether its AI models engage in subversive behavior, but restrictions on access and disclosure raise questions about their independence.
articles.content:
OpenAI will embed safety evaluators from Apollo Research, Goodfire, METR, and Transluce in its organization as part of a pilot,
OpenAI said
Monday. The news follows a series of safety incidents, including one in which an OpenAI agent swarm broke out of its sandbox and hacked into Hugging Face during cybersecurity testing. Many AI safety researchers, including from Apollo, have argued such an event might have been avoided if outside evaluators had been embedded within OpenAI to monitor its safety testing.
OpenAI said the efforts support its commitments to rely on independent assessments of safety controls under the
White House Accord on Super Intelligence.
The pilots will begin at different points, with Apollo’s beginning this week, according to OpenAI.
The idea of embedding evaluators into frontier AI labs
first came from Anthropic
, which last month started to give
METR researchers employee-level access
to its systems. Until recently, AI companies have only brought in outside reviewers to test models after post-training and shortly before public release.
Evaluators say
this is insufficient because it doesn’t allow them to test for misaligned behaviors like scheming during training or to monitor internal deployment use cases that could still pose a threat.
The work with each third-party firm differs in scope. The pilot with
OpenAI and Apollo
will focus on investigating whether models attempt to subvert their own or their successors’ alignment or control mechanisms. In other words, they’ll be on the lookout for whether AI models try to undermine the safety rules and safeguards designed to keep them, or future versions of themselves, under human control. OpenAI
recently published
findings that while training GPT-5.6 Sol, it began leaving instructions for future versions of itself telling them to conceal mistakes and misaligned behavior from the user.
Per Apollo, the pilot will examine whether training incentivizes subversion; whether evaluations can elicit subversion; whether subversion occurs during internal deployment; and whether reasoning relevant to subversion would be detectable. These risks are becoming increasingly important to monitor as AI models grow more capable of acting autonomously and deceiving humans. Apollo’s previous research with OpenAI found that models can behave differently when they know they’re being tested and tend to prioritize what evaluators want to see over users’ actual institutions.
Goodfire will embed researchers who specialize in understanding how AI models work internally. Using its interpretability platform, the firm will help OpenAI monitor training runs, fix undesired behavior, and improve alignment,
per the company.
Goodfire says it will publish findings, though its primary audience will be OpenAI’s own researchers.
With METR, OpenAI plans to perform two evaluations: one that looks for unintended or dangerous behavior in the model itself, including problems OpenAI’s own tests might have missed, and another that tests whether OpenAI’s systems are capable of catching that behavior. For the first evaluation, METR will largely decide for itself what to investigate and how to test the model. OpenAI and METR have not yet come to a decision on the scope of the second assessment, according to OpenAI.
Transluce, meanwhile, will examine whether OpenAI’s post-training safety evaluations themselves are good enough. The organization is also planning to test in 2027 how OpenAI uses its safety tests to decide whether a model is safe enough to release.
At a time when the independence of third-party evaluations is under scrutiny, it’s worth noting that Apollo and Goodfire are both receiving financial compensation for their evaluations. METR and Transluce aren’t, but they may accept compute or API credits.
Apollo, which published the most detailed account of its agreement with OpenAI, offers a closer look at the scope and limitations of these evaluations.
Many in the AI safety community have warned that AI labs might try to stymy evaluators’ independence, especially if outsiders find unflattering evidence that labs would rather keep hidden. Apollo says an essential part of the pilot is OpenAI’s agreement that the firm can publicly explain the conditions and limitations of its work.
Still, there are areas where Apollo believes its access to OpenAI’s systems is lacking. For a truly independent evaluation of the company’s AI models, Apollo says it needs true employee-level access to OpenAI’s systems, including “all data, records and documentation relevant to their assessment even if a developer was trying to hide unfavorable information.” Getting access to all data, including training data and evaluation logs which companies are loathe to show to outsiders, is important for, say, checking a company’s claims about how a model performed or determining when certain concerning behavior emerged.
In previous coverage, John Steidley, chief of staff at Palisade Research,
told TechCrunch
that it’s important to see this data in order to assess whether a model was trained to perform well on a “shutdown resistance benchmark.”
In OpenAI’s first pilot, the AI lab is providing Apollo with access to only the information required to assess whether the models engage in subversion attempts. This includes “relevant training code and datasets, reinforcement-learning rollouts with available reasoning traces and rewards, and the ability to query intermediate model checkpoints.”
The scope of access will be limited to “only the agreed claims and only for the specific models and time periods agreed for the assessment,” Apollo says. OpenAI still reserves the right to withhold certain information within that scope if it deems it necessary because of technical infeasibility, security risks, or IP protection. The company agreed not to withhold information simply because it is unfavorable.
Apollo also won’t get access to all OpenAI staffers, instead being limited to “only authorized staff,” which are participants that the AI lab selects, though Apollo can suggest certain individuals. Crucially, if an OpenAI employee outside this group raises confidential information within the scope of Apollo’s research, the firm cannot follow up and will need to cease communication and route follow-up through OpenAI.
That condition is significant. It comes in the wake of
OpenAI firing three researchers
for allegedly sharing confidential information with safety evaluation firm METR — which performed the Hugging Face incident
post-mortem
alongside independent AI safety research group Redwood.
Buck Shlegeris, CEO of Redwood, said in a post on Monday that the agreements announced don’t meet the bar of granting third parties “employee-like access,” saying it’s “disappointing but not surprising.”
OpenAI said that they'd have embedded evaluations with employee-like access; the agreements announced today obviously don't meet that bar.
This is disappointing but not surprising.
Maybe future agreements will be better.
https://t.co/kmDbg1Dqav
— Buck Shlegeris (@bshlgrs)
November 16, 2026
The pilot will also be limited in how much researchers can disclose. While Apollo will be allowed to publish independent conclusions of its findings, OpenAI will be able to limit evidence available to substantiate them publicly, which could make it hard for outsiders to independently assess the findings. Apollo has pushed back against this limitation, saying it believes researchers should be allowed to disclose the findings of the evaluation “to an appropriate outside audience even if the developer was trying to prevent the disclosure of unfavorable findings.”
That said, while the public cannot see the full supporting evidence, OpenAI says its Safety and Security Committee, which oversees safety on behalf of the OpenAI Foundation’s board, will get to review unredacted assessment reports and can communicate privately with evaluators.
While OpenAI is not granting all of Apollo’s conditions for a truly independent evaluation, the firm says the pilot is “an ambitious first step towards deeper access and disclosure rights,” and that it is working toward running full embedded evaluations with multiple AI developers in the future.

articles.title: OpenAI releases a new image classifier and ChatGPT warnings to combat CSAM
articles.summary: ChatGPT will ban an account trying to access CSAM content for 24 hours as a warning.
articles.content:
OpenAI today announced new tools to combat child sexual abuse material (CSAM) amid growing safety concerns around the use of AI tools. These features include a new image classifier to detect CSAM, warnings and temporary blocks to prevent users from creating or accessing content that sexualizes children, a new guideline for developers, and a set of tools for law enforcement.
The company unveiled a new image classifier that can detect CSAM images, including the ones generated by AI. OpenAI is giving select companies access to its classifier through its API at no cost. The tool looks for visual signs of abuse in images not seen before and assigns a score that can give an indicative direction to reviewers about dealing with CSAM.
OpenAI said that it developed this classifier with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), and it is working with
Tech Coalition
and
ROOST
to share access to the tool. In its early testing with partners, the AI company found that the classifier flags 48% fewer images while finding the same number of abusive images, reducing the work of reviewers. Plus, images flagged by the classifier are twice as likely to be abusive images.
What’s more, the company is adding new warning screens in ChatGPT to prevent users from accessing material that sexualizes children. ChatGPT will show an alert to users attempting such prompts, direct users toward specialized support to stop harmful behavior, and also suspend the account for 24 hours as a warning. The app already blocks CSAM content and requests related to it. It said that repeated offences could lead to the account being removed permanently.
OpenAI noted that it formed the message and guidelines around this behavior with organizations and researchers, including
Protect Children
, the
Lucy Faithfull Foundation
, and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who
independently evaluated a trial
of deterrent messages.
The company is also publishing guidelines for developers using OpenAI tools to prevent, detect, and help users report CSAM content. It said that in early testing, the guidelines have helped a number of developers adopt child safety tooling and register to report CSAM to NCMEC. OpenAI is also equipping law enforcement dealing with child safety with AI-powered features like dedicated plug-ins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators. It is also providing training to investigators along with a field guide on how to use AI.
OpenAI has had
several
lawsuits
against the company
blaming its technology for harming users, especially children. Safety-focused nonprofit Common Sense Media labeled OpenAI’s tech as “unacceptable risk” for teens. Other AI chatbots — specifically Grok — have been used to create nonconsensual sexualized imagery,
including of children
.
The AI startup had made changes in the last 12 months to its technology, including releasing
a safety blueprint
, updating content guidelines to
bar inappropriate content
, retuning its model to prevent them from
generating harmful content
, and releasing
a special version of ChatGPT for teens
.

articles.title: Audible turns to AI to help users discover audiobooks
articles.summary: Audible's new AI-generated audio previews summarize a book's themes and what readers liked about it, in addition to playing the narrated sample.
articles.content:
Amazon-owned audiobook service Audible is turning to AI to help listeners find their next book. The company on Monday
launched
a new “audio discovery” feature that provides a brief overview of a book’s themes and a summary of what readers liked about it, as well as commentary from an Audible editor or an author, in addition to playing the narrated sample.
The overview audio itself is generated using AI, and the commentary is pulled from recordings of past Audible interviews, the company says.
The idea is that this type of expanded introduction to a story could help users decide what to listen to next, particularly when they’re on the go and don’t have time to scroll through comments or reviews.
The feature follows
last month’s launch of a handful of AI tools
that let users engage more with the story, interact with characters, or catch up with the help of recaps. These features have come as Audible faces new competition in the audiobooks market, namely from Spotify, which introduced audiobook listening hours as part of its paid subscriptions. That service
expanded last month to over 180 markets.
Audible’s new feature takes a cue from how Amazon is already using AI to help people shop: On the Amazon storefront, AI can summarize buyers’ product reviews so shoppers can get a quick sense of what people had to say, as well as the pros and cons of a particular item. In Audible’s case, it’s pulling information about what people liked about the book from publicly available reviews.
But such a feature could limit users’ exposure to negative reviews if the AI only pulls information from those that offer positive remarks. (Further testing will be needed to see if this is the case, of course.)
Audible says the overviews will also draw on other publicly available materials, like synopses and metadata.
The feature will initially be available for select English-language titles in the U.S., and will arrive alongside new personalized collections based on users’ listening taste that could help them find other books.
The company’s other recent AI features, Recaps and the interactive “Ask a Question” tool, are also now expanding to more U.S. titles, and will become more broadly available in December. These features will only be available to customers who have purchased a title or who have access to the book as part of their Audible membership, the company said.
“Picking your next listen should feel like getting a tip from a friend,” said Andy Tsao, Audible’s chief product and analytics officer, in a statement. “With audio discovery, you’ll get a quick audio take on why the title might be right for you from our editors, fellow listeners, or even the author. Some of the best listening experiences are those rare finds or hidden gems, and we want to make those great discoveries happen more often and more easily,” he added.

articles.title: US tightens AI chip export controls to deter Chinese companies from accessing compute remotely
articles.summary: Under the interim rule, the U.S. will require firms to get licenses to export AI chips if they may provide compute to China or other restricted countries.
articles.content:
The Trump administration on Monday is preparing to roll out new export controls on AI chips and data centers outside the U.S., seeking to prevent companies, especially those in China, from getting past U.S. export controls by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries.
Under the
interim rule
, the Commerce Department will require companies to get licenses to export, reexport, or transfer AI chips and servers to data centers anywhere in the world if they may provide compute to companies in China or other restricted countries.
The remote-access rules target companies based in the U.S.’s D:5 group of embargoed countries, which includes China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and 18 others.
The U.S. already has rules requiring chip companies to get a license to ship AI chips to companies based in, or owned by any business in, this group of countries.
“This new control is a logical extension of existing controls,” the interim rule reads. “These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models.”
The move comes days after
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned
amid a scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy linked to one of the chipmaker’s customers. The U.S. government has reportedly been wanting to put that customer, Megaspeed, on a special entity list, as it believes the company has been buying thousands of Nvidia chips to
provide compute
to Chinese businesses to get past existing export-control restrictions.
Reuters
reported last week
that Chinese AI companies are rushing to secure computing capacity overseas amid fears of tighter restrictions from the U.S.
The rule applies to data centers or any network that can supply over 12 million total processing performance (TPP), an export-control metric the U.S. uses to measure computing power. (Twelve million TPP roughly works out to the max computing power of about 750 Nvidia H100 or H200 chips.) The rule also covers indirect access through go-betweens or brokers, and exporters and data center operators are required to keep an eye on their customers’ ownership structures and activities to ensure they aren’t run by anyone from the D:5 group.
The rule also adds new licensing requirements for chip exports, reexports, or transfer of advanced semiconductors to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil. The Commerce Department said it had included these as they “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.” For these countries, however, the license requirements will not apply to chips “destined” for companies based in the U.S.
Existing data center operators providing services that fall under this new rule are required to get licenses within 90 days of the rule coming into effect.
Notably, the rule doesn’t apply to commercial recommendation systems, like those used in e-commerce or social media.
The rule also rescinds the Biden admin’s AI Diffusion Rule from January 2025, which sought to impose country-level limits on exports of advanced AI chips, and restrict transfers of certain powerful AI models. That May, the Trump administration said it would throw out that framework, arguing that it added unnecessary restrictions on U.S. companies and the country’s allies.
“By making these changes, this IFR prevents the use of certain SI items in data centers and at a computing power level that can be used for training or running of advanced SI models,” the rule reads. “Access to such computing power can be used to train and run advanced SI models capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten U.S. national security or foreign policy interests.”

articles.title: Google Maps can now build trip itineraries with real-time details about each stop
articles.summary: You could use Ask Maps to plan a holiday shopping day trip or something more complex, like a three-day road trip featuring coastal hikes and oceanfront dining.
articles.content:
Google
announced
on Monday that it’s rolling out new Maps features that are designed to help people plan trips and everyday tasks using AI. The company is launching the ability for Maps to create trip itineraries and find appointments for users.
The new features reflect a broader shift in how tech companies are positioning AI, which is less as a tool that just answers questions and more as an assistant that can complete tasks on users’ behalf. While many companies have released AI agents to complete these tasks, Google is working to bring that approach into a service that millions of people already use every day.
Google says users can use the navigation platform’s
“Ask Maps”
tool to build step-by-step trip itineraries and get real-time details about their route right when they pull up directions.
Image Credits:
Google
For example, you could use Ask Maps to plan a holiday shopping day trip or something more complex, like a three-day road trip featuring coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Google says. You’ll get a day-by-day itinerary with insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop. Once you’re happy with your itinerary, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop.
When you’re ready to head out, you can use Ask Maps to reopen your itinerary or find the “itinerary” badge in your chat history. You’ll have access to real-time information, including traffic conditions, business hours, and a look at what the “vibe” is at your next stop, the company says. You could also adjust your schedule by asking Maps to do something like add a scenic viewpoint or lunch stop along your route. You can then tap any destination in your itinerary to get directions and navigate to your next stop.
Additionally, users can use Ask Maps to find beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments online and call local businesses for you. For example, you could ask: “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me.” Ask Maps will then display open slots across nearby businesses.
Image Credits:
Google
The new agentic calling feature arrives as tech companies continue to introduce AI agents designed to handle time-consuming tasks, such as scheduling DMV appointments and making reservations. For example,
Meta’s AI agent Muse

articles.title: Freshworks alums raise $53M to take on Salesforce, HubSpot with AI-native CRM
articles.summary: Dreamteam has signed up more than 100 customers across 13 countries, with some businesses switching from established CRMs.
articles.content:
Dreamteam
, a startup founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million to challenge Salesforce and HubSpot with its AI-native CRM, betting that AI can finally shake up a market where established players have so far proved difficult to dislodge.
The funding comprises seed and Series A rounds, led by Together Fund and Accel respectively, with participation from Premji Invest. The San Francisco-based startup declined to disclose the size of each round or its valuation.
Traditional CRMs depend on salespeople to manually record customer interactions and keep deal information up to date. That often leaves businesses with incomplete or outdated information. Dreamteam aims to eliminate much of that work by automatically capturing context from sources including emails and customer conversations. It also uses AI agents to handle tasks such as follow-ups, meeting preparation, and pipeline monitoring.
Dreamteam co-founder and CEO Anand Venkatraman (pictured above, right) told TechCrunch that he had repeatedly encountered problems with traditional CRM platforms over more than 25 years in enterprise software, including at Salesforce and Freshworks. Salespeople spent considerable time updating records, yet managers still struggled to get a reliable picture of their business. “In all these years, I have never come across an instance where I could click a button and get a forecast from the CRM,” he said.
That experience led Venkatraman to co-found Dreamteam in 2025 with Senthil Kanthaswamy (pictured above, center), who spent more than nine years at Freshworks, most recently as a product leader at Freshservice, and Ramesh Parthasarathy (pictured above, left), who previously worked on AI and platform engineering at Freshworks.
At the heart of Dreamteam’s CRM is what it calls the Company Brain. This acts as virtual memory, pulling together information from emails, meetings, and other customer interactions to build a shared record of customer relationships. Four built-in AI agents use that information to research prospects, draft follow-up emails, flag potential risks to deals, and configure CRM workflows, with sales teams retaining control over what gets sent to customers.
Dreamteam has signed up more than 100 customers across 13 countries in the three months since it began actively selling its product, with most paying for the service, Venkatraman said. The startup has also replaced established CRM platforms at several businesses, including Salesforce at healthcare company DMS Health and HubSpot at other customers.
The advertising sales team at media streaming company Plex also chose Dreamteam over HubSpot and other AI-native CRM alternatives, Venkatraman told TechCrunch. Plex’s co-founder and chief product officer Scott Olechowski said Dreamteam’s ability to integrate with AI tools already used across the company was a “game changer.”
Replacing established CRM platforms at scale may prove more difficult. In a blog post earlier this year, venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z)
argued
that while AI could transform how businesses manage customer relationships, existing CRMs are likely to remain the systems where customer records are stored, with a new generation of AI-powered tools capturing much of the value by working on top of them.
Venkatraman acknowledged that Salesforce and HubSpot are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, but noted that their entrenched positions do not guarantee they will dominate the next generation of CRM software.
“We see this as an electric-car moment for systems of record,” he said, adding that AI requires a fundamental rethink of how CRMs are built — not simply adding new features to existing platforms.
Kanthaswamy believes startups have a window of two to five years to gain ground before established CRM providers can fully adapt to AI. Rebuilding software around a fundamentally different architecture takes time, he stated, giving newer companies an opportunity to attract customers while incumbents work to overhaul their existing products.
Dreamteam also plans to expand beyond sales into other parts of the customer lifecycle, including onboarding, customer support, and upselling. The startup already has a feature called Magic Apps that allows users to create custom applications and dashboards within the CRM using natural-language instructions, without writing code.
Currently, Dreamteam employs more than 35 people, with its engineering team based in Chennai and its go-to-market operations in the United States. Kanthaswamy said the startup aims to reach eight figures in annual revenue by the end of 2027, though he declined to disclose the startup’s current revenue.

Emma Roth
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.
Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation from Nvidia after more than 33 years has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry. Now prominent figures are calling for Huang’s reinstatement, and many are also hopping on board with a theory spreading throughout Silicon Valley: that the scandal is the result of a plot against the former CEO.
At the center of this theory is the
reporting from
The
New York Times
that former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, one of multiple women Huang is accused of having an affair with, is a Chinese spy.
US agencies haven’t confirmed
whether this is the case, and
President Donald Trump claims he was unaware
of any spy allegations. Jensen Huang’s alleged relationship with Alice Huang
set off the events that led to his resignation; s
ubsequent reporting suggested he had an affair with two employees
at Nvidia
, including one of his direct reports. The revelation raised new questions around whether Nvidia customers, including Megaspeed, were
funneling chips
to China in circumvention of export restrictions. Last year, Nvidia intervened in a chip-smuggling probe surrounding the Singapore-based company,
according to
Bloomberg
.
David Sacks, a venture capitalist and former White House AI crypto advisor, has made it clear that he’s skeptical about
The New York Times
’ reporting. In
a post on X, Sacks
points to an
article from CNN
, which says US officials still can’t confirm that Alice Huang was a spy. “The spy narrative is collapsing already,” Sacks writes. He continued to question the spy allegations during
Semafor
’s Silicon Valley & The World event on Monday,
saying
: “The reason why Jensen lost his job is because of this lurid Chinese spy allegation. So if no one’s willing to back that up now, then again, I question why this entire chain of events happened.”
Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney similarly expressed concern about how Huang’s resignation played out. In a reply to Sacks’ post about the CNN article, Sweeney
said
, “What?! So journalists with sketchy motives portrayed rumors from god-knows-who (lobbyists?) as facts sourced from intelligence officials and gaslit the NVIDIA board to push out the founder, CEO, and once-in-generation visionary?” Amjad Masad, the CEO of the AI app and website builder Replit,
called the timing
of Huang’s resignation “suspicious,” adding that “if Jensen, the premier champion of open models, is taken out then anyone who wants AI closed, centralized, and controlled might benefit.”
SemiAnalysis, a research and consulting firm for the semiconductor and AI industry, posted a “conspiracy theory take on the situation,”
speculating
that Huang’s removal is a way to “remove opposition to an extremely hawkish China export control bill,” referring to the Remote Access Security Act (RASA). The bill, which Huang opposed, would extend AI export controls to cloud servers that allow companies in restricted countries to rent access to Nvidia’s AI chips. The Department of Commerce
released an interim final rule on Monday
in an attempt to address this loophole.
Related
The Nvidia scandal isn’t slowing down
What could China get from Jensen Huang?
More than 185,000 people, including Sweeney, Masad, Elon Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke,
have signed a “Stand with Jensen” letter
, calling for his reinstatement as CEO. The letter similarly calls for a closer look into the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation. “We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the center of this controversy was a spy,” the letter says. “Suspicion or association alone is not a sufficient basis for ending Jensen’s leadership. The inquiry must establish the facts, not merely justify an outcome already imposed.”

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is once again addressing his controversial comments on PC RAM purchases. “I want to be clear, I want people to have a lot of RAM, I think everybody should be able to buy a lot of RAM for their own computer,” Altman said today. “I think the home tinkering is great.”
The comments were

summit on Monday.
Altman’s remarks on RAM stirred up controversy last month. In an appearance

Cheeky Pint
podcast

earlier this month

AI companies have been buying up the world’s memory supply for data centers, leading to ongoing price hikes on everything from
phones

game consoles

I think it would be much better if the world just had a lot of memory. That comment, which I think got misinterpreted, but there is a true part of it, which I will stand by is that, if we’re going to be in this memory supply shortage, then in some sense — whether or not we’ll decide to do it, because I think there are other tradeoffs like people having their own at-home inference — the optimal thing would be, can we share this memory and have it working 100 percent of the time rather than sometimes off in someone’s edge device? Again, optimal use of this limited supply. Maybe it’s not the reason to make the decision but that’s what I was trying to say.”
Altman also
commented on Jensen Huang’s resignation

They may have a point.﻿
They may have a point.﻿
by
Ellen Thomas
Nov 16, 2026, 8:29 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Constellation’s Clinton Clean Energy Center’s single nuclear reactor power plant, July 25, 2025 in Clinton, Illinois. Meta signed a 20-year power purchase agreement with Constellation for the output from the plant.
Image: Getty Images
Part Of

see all
Ellen Thomas
is an independent reporter focused on business investigations, analysis and news. She previously covered the AI data center boom for Business Insider.
Constellation Energy – America’s largest operator of nuclear power plants – does not share Wall Street’s concerns that the Democrats will slow down data center development. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week, CEO Joe Dominguez was, for lack of a better word, unbothered as he addressed the blue wave.
“I do think we’ve seen a bit of an overreaction in the market to the election results based upon fear that Democrats won’t let data centers get built,” Dominguez said.
Many of the Democrats who seized control of the House and Senate in this month’s midterm elections ran on anti-data-center campaigns, which triggered a
historic $2.5 trillion sell-off
in AI-adjacent stocks that reached well beyond tech to the energy, construction, and materials sectors.
Up until a few years ago, many of Constellation’s nuclear power plants were in severe financial distress and in danger of shutting down early. But the data center development boom and its enormous demand for electricity have dramatically reversed the nuclear industry’s fate.
Related
Lame-duck Congress might actually do something: speed up energy projects
Data centers lost the midterms
Data centers want to suck everything dry — even the desert
Now, Constellation and other companies like it are signing major deals with Big Tech companies to provide power to data centers. Microsoft, for instance, signed a deal with Constellation to fund the revival of a nuclear plant at Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania. (Three Mile Island is the site of what the Nuclear Regulatory Commission
refers to
as the “most serious accident in US commercial nuclear power plant operating history.”)
Constellation also signed major contracts in the third quarter to provide power to Amazon and Google data centers, Dominguez said.
Nuclear energy has had bipartisan support for years. The US Department of Energy
classifies
nuclear as a “clean” energy source because the act of operating a nuclear reactor does not directly produce carbon emissions. This makes nuclear an appealing investment to Big Tech companies that have to balance aggressive data center development with the ambitious climate goals they set long before the AI race took off. Still, nuclear energy has its issues. One of the biggest is nuclear waste, which the US government
has not figured out
how to dispose of at scale.
Big Nuclear and Big Tech also tout these deals as good for the economy and job creation.
“The market scare that people got last week was not lost on Democrats,” Dominguez said on the call. “They do not want to be the reason that the economy takes a nosedive by halting data center development.”
Of course, Constellation’s future is essentially staked on the data center buildout, and Dominguez’s job is to convince investors they have nothing to worry about.
In this instance, however, Dominguez really does seem genuinely unconcerned by the new Democratic majority in the federal government. It could be that he understands that, yes, while the Democrats
won the midterms
on promises of data center regulation
and the blue wave included many new Democratic governors, data centers aren’t necessarily a strictly partisan issue. Some Democrats
have opposed harsh measures like moratoriums
— though on the flip slide, Constellation may also have to deal with challenges from the other side of the aisle.
In Virginia, some of the state lawmakers who have been the most vocal about data centers are actually Republican. Virginia Sen. Richard Stuart, a conservative Republican, has aggressively pursued data center regulation. Last month, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, denied Stuart’s
request
for a special session to address a concerning new report from the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality on the state’s groundwater supply, which has become strained amid rampant data center growth.
For years, companies like Constellation have been sitting on a bunch of old reactors teetering on the edge of extinction because they didn’t have enough customers to keep them afloat.
The fight against data centers so far has been highly fragmented and hyperlocal, but that could change soon. The Trump administration loves data centers, and the federal government is working on wresting some control over data center development away from the states. But even then, Democrats and Republicans at the federal level tend to view data centers as an inevitable part of the future that needs some guardrails rather than out-of-control corporate growth infringing on the average American’s quality of life.
Just look at the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which was co-sponsored by two Democrats. The Senate is expected to
vote on a passage
of
a sweeping bill
which is being marketed as a way to speed up the permitting process for new power plants and transmission lines and connect new data centers to the grid faster. New Mexico Sen. Martin Heinrich, one of the Democrats backing the bill, has touted its inclusion of provisions designed to protect utility customers from rising rates due to data centers, ensuring Big Tech pays its fair share of costs. Researchers at Columbia University SIPA’s Center on Global Energy Policy called the bill’s protections “
mixed
,” noting they do not account for wholesale capacity and energy prices, a “principal way” data center electricity demand can lead to higher household bills.
Senate Democrats are sharply divided on the bill, which critics say will fast-track data center projects at the expense of public input and environmental oversight and lead to a massive overbuild of energy projects that Americans will end up paying for.
On Constellation’s earnings call, Dominguez pointed out that Virginia and Illinois, states with Democratic governors already in place before the election, have seen “a great deal of data center development.”
“The bottom line is that Democrats care deeply about economic growth and they care very deeply about the many labor jobs that go with data center construction,” Dominguez said. “With labor such a key constituent for Democrats, it’s hard to imagine that we are going to halt work …There might be some differences and certainly there are going to be some local areas, I think, that are not going to want data centers.”
Of course, Dominguez is speaking to investors here, and he wants to assuage their concerns. He also has a good point. Grassroots efforts to stop local data center development have been successful and have contributed to broader opposition to data center development across the country. But data center developers can also abandon projects and go elsewhere. Until a few years ago, data centers were largely concentrated in Northern Virginia, but with the AI boom, developers have fanned out across the country in search of available power and land. A total of 38 states have
welcomed them
with open arms and generous tax breaks, per the National Conference of State Legislatures.
Of course, Dominguez is speaking to investors here, and he wants to assuage their concerns.
Thanks to the convoluted way the US electric grid and energy markets work, Constellation’s power plants don’t even need to be located in the same state as their data center customers — the plant supplying the power just needs to be connected to the same region from which the grid is drawing power. The purchase agreement, in that sense, is symbolic: Because the data center needs more electricity than it can draw from the local grid without causing disruptions for everyone else, the data center pays for independent power providers like Constellation to supply the grid with extra electricity.
That’s why data centers and the enormous amount of electricity Big Tech says it needs to power them have been such a boon for the nuclear industry. For years, companies like Constellation have been sitting on a bunch of old reactors teetering on the edge of extinction because they didn’t have enough customers to keep them afloat.
Nuclear lobbyists will tell you that’s because the NRC’s safety regulations are overly restrictive and lead to untenable upfront capital costs that make projects impossible to finance. (This has been an industry talking point since 1979, after the NRC seriously overhauled its safety standards following the partial meltdown at Three Mile Island. That site is now owned by Constellation, which has signed a 20-year deal with Microsoft.)
Both the Biden and Trump administrations have worked to support the development of nuclear power in the US by passing developer tax credits. The Trump administration has gone even further, pushing for a sweeping reform of the NRC that would make it much easier for new reactors to obtain operating licenses.
And the Department of Energy this month approved a $5 billion loan to Constellation, which the company will use to upgrade its existing nuclear fleet. Another nuclear energy company, Vistra, received a $4.2 billion loan.
It’s not totally unlike the Biden administration’s passage of the Civil Nuclear Credit Program in 2022, which planned to loan $6 billion to struggling nuclear companies in the US.
That’s not lost on Dominguez.
“Interestingly, in many respects the election had the Republicans saying a lot of the same things that the Democrats were saying,” Dominguez told investors on the call. “And I believe that the policy solutions are going to be somewhat similar.”
