Justine Calma
is a senior science reporter covering energy and the environment with more than a decade of experience. She is also the host of
Hell or High Water: When Disaster Hits Home
, a podcast from Vox Media and Audible Originals.
Fossil fuels are still the biggest source of electricity for hyperscale data centers in the US, a new
paper
published in the journal
Nature Sustainability
shows. They likely burn through more electricity collectively than many countries do, resulting in a serious amount of greenhouse gas emissions.
The study homes in on hyperscale facilities — the massive structures spanning millions of square feet that developers are racing to build in large part to support generative AI. Researchers say the findings show that there’s a lot of work left to do to cut down pollution stemming from AI’s reliance on fossil fuels.
“We tend to discuss AI’s environmental footprint as though it were some fixed property of the technology, when in reality the same computing infrastructure can have dramatically different consequences depending on the electricity system supporting it,” Gianluca Guidi, lead author of the new study and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, says in an email to
The Verge.
“I actually find that encouraging, because it means these impacts aren’t inevitable. We have choices about where we build and how we power this infrastructure.”
“The same computing infrastructure can have dramatically different consequences depending on the electricity system supporting it.”
Guidi and his team used satellite imagery to identify 403 hyperscale data centers in the US, estimating each facility’s power consumption based on its electrical capacity. Using data from the Environmental Protection Agency, they approximated how much carbon pollution each data center would have produced if connected to the local power grid between May 2024 and April 2025.
Altogether, the 403 hyperscale facilities likely consumed around 82 terawatt-hours of electricity that year, about 1.8 percent of all US electricity consumption. That’s even more than the amount of electricity that about 148 nations — a majority of the countries in the world including Austria, Israel, and Venezuela but excluding the largest economies including the US and China — individually burn through each year, according to John Sterman, director of the MIT System Dynamics group and MIT Sloan Sustainability Initiative.
Electricity demand from these data centers produced 25.7 million metric tons of CO2 emissions, comparable to the annual carbon footprint of Denmark, according to the research paper. Sterman says that exceeds the total carbon emissions of about 113 nations. That’s because about 54 percent of the electricity the hyperscale facilities consumed likely came from gas and coal.
Sterman, who was not involved in the research with Guidi, disclosed that he used the help of Claude to compare the paper’s findings to electricity use and emissions of countries. “I think AI can be extraordinarily helpful,” Sterman says. “But we’ve got to figure out a way to limit the harms … Especially because those impacts are irreversible. Once you allow these data centers to emit the CO2, you can never undo that.”
Sterman says policymakers should require data center operators to bring new clean energy online. The study doesn’t account for local air pollution that can result from new gas infrastructure that’s being built to meet data center demand, or gas turbines that some AI companies have installed at their facilities to power themselves without connecting to the grid. And while hyperscale data centers encompass more than just AI-related computing, they also make up just a fraction of the
thousands of data centers in the US
— with more cropping up each year.
Related
The global pledge to use AI for climate good is a cruel joke
The study showed how big a difference the local electricity mix makes when it comes to the environmental impact of AI and data centers. Generating electricity in heavily coal-reliant Wyoming led to roughly seven times more carbon emissions per kilowatt-hour than in hydropower-rich Oregon. “Two data centers consuming exactly the same amount of electricity can have dramatically different carbon footprints simply because of where they’re located,” Guidi writes.
Fengqi You, a professor in energy systems engineering at Cornell University who was also not involved in the study, says the results highlight the problem of “long-term carbon lock-in.” “Power plants and supporting infrastructure built to meet rapidly growing data center demand may operate for decades. Decisions made today could therefore shape emissions well into the future,” You says in an email to
The Verge.
Both You and Guidi also pointed out how problematic it is that researchers have to go through such great lengths to estimate energy consumption because data center operators won’t disclose that information. To that end, Guidi and his colleagues are using their research to build a
website
to track the environmental impact of individual data centers. A
bipartisan bill making its way through Congress
could also mandate greater disclosures nationally on data centers’ electricity use.
“Communities and policymakers need reliable, independent data on what these facilities mean for our air, health, and the climate. This study is an important step.” Gina McCarthy, former White House national climate advisor and EPA administrator, said in a statement shared by the research authors.

Lauren Feiner
is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.
OpenAI is
announcing
a tool that it says will help child sexual abuse investigators cut through the noise to find harmful material they can act on quickly.
At a Monday press briefing in Washington, DC, OpenAI announced a classifier it says can better detect abusive imagery of kids, including whether it’s AI-generated. It’s also offering free access to vetted organizations, giving developers more guidance on how to detect this type of content, and helping to train law enforcement on how AI can aid their investigations. The news comes as policymakers and others are pushing for more safety restrictions on AI tools, accusing OpenAI and other companies of facilitating harm to children.
In recent years, AI-generated sexual images of children have threatened to overwhelm systems like the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) CyberTipline, which collects and triages reports of child sexual abuse material (CSAM). The CyberTipline
received
400,000 generative AI-related reports in 2025, an exponential increase from the 67,000 it received in 2024, and
researchers have warned
that the influx could make NCMEC’s workload “unmanageable.” The US government
has stated
that both AI-generated and non-AI-generated CSAM is illegal, and
48 states have laws
to address sexually explicit AI deepfakes. But the tools to make them are
widely available
, and researchers say that a flood of fake images can make it harder to tell when a child is actively experiencing harm.
The influx of AI-generated CSAM reports to NCMEC is “explosive”
North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson, who cochairs the
AG Alliance’s AI Task Force
, said at OpenAI’s event that the influx of AI-generated CSAM reports to NCMEC is “explosive” — and if they keep going that way, “it is going to mean that we fail in our mission.” Tech companies are facing a range of policy proposals that could require them to take more action against CSAM and other potentially harmful content for kids.
The Take It Down Act
now requires social media platforms to remove real or AI-generated nonconsensual intimate images within 48 hours, and the newly elected Congress could seek to take stronger action against AI companies like SpaceXSI, whose Grok chatbot went on an
undressing spree
earlier this year. Last month eight states
sued OpenAI
for a separate set of alleged harms to children, citing lawsuits alleging ChatGPT encouraged illegal substance use and suicide.
OpenAI says its classifier dramatically cuts down on false positives, flagging 48 percent fewer images, while the images it did identify were twice as likely to contain abusive material. It’s designed to catch abusive AI-generated images produced by a variety of tools, including open-source models and nudifying apps. It’s also the first broadly available CSAM classifier with a specific flag for AI-generated material, said OpenAI’s head of child safety public policy, John Buckley, at the briefing. “It’s important for industry to be able to understand what images may contain a fictional child versus a real child,” Buckley added. “That triage is critical in law enforcement reporting flows.” He also emphasized, however, that laws should recognize the harm of AI-generated CSAM: “It potentially erodes social norms in offending against children, and it’s often found colocated with child sexual abuse imagery of real children,” Buckley said.
OpenAI says its classifier dramatically cuts down on false positives, flagging 48 percent fewer images
OpenAI’s own ChatGPT image generator is designed to deny user requests for CSAM. Now, users who attempt to produce it will be shown a new warning developed with expert guidance to try to encourage them to seek help. A first offense will trigger a 24-hour pause in accessing ChatGPT and warn the user their account could be permanently closed, while offering support resources to combat the behavior. OpenAI
says it reports
“all instances of CSAM” to NCMEC. In a statement, Buckley explained that the 24-hour pause is based on expert advice for best practices “and international evidence on what works to prevent and respond to CSAM seeking vs CSAM generation.” The point is “to interrupt harmful behavior and direct people toward specialist help to stop it.”
Jackson said that North Carolina and many other states now have laws that cover synthetic CSAM, but that partnering with a tech company like OpenAI to help deter its creation is a fairly novel approach to an emerging issue. “Most of what AGs do is accountability work,” he told reporters at the briefing. “Most of our jurisdiction kicks in after the fact to hold people accountable for harm. But with this, we wanted to see if it was possible to develop a model of working together to prevent that harm. And I would say it’s still basically an experiment.”

articles.title: Windows 11 Is Collecting Data on Which Coding Agents and Developer Tools You Use
articles.content:
Title: Windows 11 Is Collecting Data on Which Coding Agents and Developer Tools You Use

URL Source: https://xusheng.dev/posts/windows-coding-agent-telemetry/

Published Time: 2026-11-16 00:00:00 -0500 EST

Markdown Content:
Reverse engineering Windows 11's MissionControlAggregator reveals coding-agent and developer-tool usage bits in a diagnostic ETW report.

I recently asked AI to help me look through the latest Windows binaries for undocumented features and functionality. Among the leads it turned up, one list immediately caught my attention: coding agents such as `codex.exe`, `claude.exe`, `copilot.exe`, and `cursor.exe`, alongside familiar developer tools such as `python.exe`, `dotnet.exe`, `gcc.exe`, and `code.exe`.

Why would a Windows system DLL need a list of coding agents and developer tools?

The names were in `MissionControlAggregator.dll`. I asked the agent to follow the references and dig into what the DLL actually does. That led from a handful of string comparisons to a running Windows component that records which coding agents and developer tools have been used, saves that information locally, and reports it to Windows Diagnostics. And unless you have opted out of the “optional” diagnostic data (which is enabled by default), the data is uploaded to Microsoft.

I [shared the initial finding on X](https://x.com/CrackmesOne/status/2122147747390468384). This post includes more details about the investigation behind it.

## Following the names

Opening the DLL in [Binary Ninja](https://binary.ninja/) made the first lead easy to see. These were explicit executable names embedded in a Windows component:

Following the references showed that the names were used in comparisons. There are four CLI-agent slots checking `copilot.exe`, `claude.exe`, `codex.exe`, and `agy.exe`, with extensionless equivalents on the WSL route. Five desktop-agent slots check `github.exe`, `claude.exe`, `codex.exe`, `cursor.exe`, and `antigravity.exe`.

Here is one of the comparisons against `codex.exe`:

The compiler-generated C++ names are unwieldy, so I will call these functions **executable-name matchers**. For reference, one related matcher is `std::_Func_impl_no_alloc<<lambda_340dfe7e962ab225b6ac33bc664bd54f>, bool, std::basic_string_view<wchar_t, std::char_traits<wchar_t>> const&, Microsoft::Diagnostics::MissionControlAggregator::Utils::AppType>::_Do_call`. The screenshot shows another lambda instantiation performing the same kind of name comparison.

The feature guarding the new agent checks has a particularly direct name: `CLICodingAgentUsage`, feature ID `62580080`.

And the list extends beyond AI agents. The same component checks for `node.exe`, `python.exe`, `dotnet.exe`, `gcc.exe`, `clang.exe`, `gdb.exe`, `javac.exe`, `devenv.exe`, and `code.exe`, among others. Those checks feed broader developer-tool categories. Some of these checks also verify the publisher: the Node.js slot expects `Node.js Foundation`, Python expects `Python Software Foundation`, and the .NET and Visual Studio slots expect `Microsoft Corporation`. The compiler/debugger group containing GCC and Clang has no additional publisher check in this path.

## Where does the DLL get this information?

The next question was whether the component scans running processes itself. Following `Aggregator::OnLoad` revealed that it subscribes to existing Windows events instead.

For Windows programs, it consumes `KernelProcess.AppStateChangeSummary` and `Win32kTraceLogging.AppInteractivitySummary`. These provide application identities that its handlers parse and pass to the matchers. For WSL, it consumes `Microsoft.Windows.Lxss.Manager.Exec` and `ExecCritical`, using the `imageName` field. A regular Windows `codex.exe` can therefore reach the CLI-agent checks through the app-state summary route; this is not limited to Linux programs running inside WSL.

The relevant flow looks like this:

```
Aggregator::OnLoad
├─ WSL Exec / ExecCritical
│  └─ ProcessWslExecEvent → CLI agent matchers
├─ KernelProcess.AppStateChangeSummary
│  └─ ProcessAppStateChangeSummaryEvent → CLI agent matchers
└─ Win32kTraceLogging.AppInteractivitySummary
   └─ ProcessAppInteractivitySummaryEvent → desktop agent matchers

Aggregator::OnRelativeTimerExpire
└─ MissionControlAggregatorLogging::ReportCohorts<12,4,5>
   └─ Segments.SubCohorts ETW report

Aggregator::OnUnload / intermediate timer
└─ PersistentState::SaveToDisk
```

Text

A successful match sets a slot in the aggregator’s state. Later, `ReportCohorts<12,4,5>` turns those slots into bitsets and emits a report named `Segments.SubCohorts`. The numbers correspond to twelve broader tool categories, four CLI agents, and five desktop agents.

[ETW (Event Tracing for Windows)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/etw/event-tracing-portal) is the mechanism carrying that report. In this case, it is a self-describing TraceLogging event. Rather than writing the executable names into every report, the component assigns each category a bit. A set Codex bit means the matching tool was observed during the reporting window.

The source events also include runtime, time in focus, interaction counters, and resource usage. This component appears to discard those details and record only a bitmap of which agents were observed. The report’s timestamps describe the collection window, not how long each agent was used.

Although I found no prompt text or source code in this report, collecting which agents and developer tools someone uses already has significant privacy implications.

## Is it actually running on a normal machine?

Strings and code are a useful lead, but I wanted to see the component running. I checked my Parallels Windows 11 ARM64 VM, build `26200.9974`. Its `MissionControlAggregator.dll` was version `10.0.26100.9818`, and `CLICodingAgentUsage` was already enabled as a service experiment. I had not manually enabled the feature.

DiagTrack, the **Connected User Experiences and Telemetry** service, was also already running with its startup type set to `Automatic`. It starts a separate `AggregatorHost.exe` process, and that process loads the DLL. The following administrative PowerShell commands show the service, its child process, and the loaded module:

```
PS> Get-Service DiagTrack | Format-Table Name,Status,StartType -AutoSize

Name       Status StartType
----       ------ ---------
DiagTrack Running Automatic

PS> Get-Process AggregatorHost | Format-Table ProcessName,Id -AutoSize

ProcessName      Id
-----------      --
AggregatorHost 1500

PS> Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter "Name='DiagTrack'" |
       Format-List Name,State,StartMode,ProcessId

Name      : DiagTrack
State     : Running
StartMode : Auto
ProcessId : 10148

PS> Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "Name='AggregatorHost.exe'" |
       Format-List ProcessId,ParentProcessId

ProcessId       : 1500
ParentProcessId : 10148

PS> tasklist /m MissionControlAggregator.dll

Image Name                     PID Modules
========================= ======== ============================================
AggregatorHost.exe            1500 MissionControlAggregator.dll
```

PowerShell

The process IDs connect the pieces: DiagTrack runs in process `10148`, which is the parent of `AggregatorHost.exe`, process `1500`; the module listing places `MissionControlAggregator.dll` inside that child.

The public ISO’s baseline VM had the coding-agent feature disabled by image default, so the evidence does not support saying that it is active on every Windows installation. On my ARM64 VM, however, the relevant feature and service were active before the test.

## Testing it in practice

To test the finding in practice, I copied `cmd.exe` to a file named `codex.exe` and ran it in the interactive Windows session. The name alone was enough for the component to recognize it as Codex.

I captured an `AppStateChangeSummary` for the running process from the `KernelProcess` provider (`{2839ff94-8f12-4e1b-82e3-af7af77a450f}`), with `LaunchCount=1` and `TerminateCount=0`. The aggregator’s saved state contained the value `2` in CLI slot 2, the Codex slot. A separate run without an additional ETW trace also set that slot, confirming that detection worked through Windows’ existing diagnostic collection.

That state is persisted in:

```
C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Diagnosis\AggregatorStorage\MissionControlAggregator$
```

Text

The report normally follows a roughly daily boundary. To capture it immediately, I temporarily moved the saved reporting-window start 25 hours into the past and restarted DiagTrack with a trace listening for the aggregator. The resulting `Segments.SubCohorts` event contained:

```
Provider: Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator
Time:     2026-11-16T12:34:29.125116Z
Version:  0.1.5

CliAgentSubCohorts:     4
DesktopAgentSubCohorts: 0
FlushedFromSave:       true
```

Text

The value `4` is `1 << 2`: the Codex CLI bit. The name had made it through the input summary, the matcher, the persisted state, and the emitted report.

I also tested the developer-tool path separately, using a copy of `cmd.exe` named `gcc.exe`. It set developer-tool slot 3. With optional diagnostic data allowed, I found the resulting `Segments.SubCohorts` event in DiagTrack’s upload queue with `SubCohorts: [8]` (`1 << 3`). This is the compiler/debugger category shared by GCC, Clang, and related tools, rather than a separate bit for each executable.

## Following the report toward Microsoft

An ETW event by itself would not establish that anything leaves the machine. ETW is used for plenty of local diagnostics. The more revealing question was who was listening to this particular report.

The VM already had a `Diagtrack-Listener` session subscribed to both ends of the path. These PowerShell queries showed its subscriptions:

```
Get-EtwTraceProvider -SessionName Diagtrack-Listener `
  -Guid '{2839ff94-8f12-4e1b-82e3-af7af77a450f}'

Get-EtwTraceProvider -SessionName Diagtrack-Listener `
  -Guid '{00de11a2-ec06-58e5-1a2b-21bb21dbee4b}'
```

PowerShell

The first subscription, for `KernelProcess`, had `MatchAnyKeyword=0x400000000002`, which includes the summary’s `0x400000000000` keyword. The second, for `Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator`, had `MatchAnyKeyword=0xe00000000000`, which includes the report’s `0x800000000000` keyword. Both had level `255`.

The subscription showed where the report could go. To check whether Windows actually queued it for transmission, I inspected DiagTrack’s `EventStore.db` and decompressed the JSON batches in its `AsimovEvents` table. This revealed an important condition: the agent-usage report is treated as **optional diagnostic data**.

**When optional diagnostic data is allowed (enabled by default in the US setup I tested), Windows queues the coding-agent usage report for upload to Microsoft.** I verified this by finding the agent event itself in DiagTrack’s upload queue:

```
{
  "name": "Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator.Segments.SubCohorts",
  "ext": {
    "privacy": { "isRequired": false }
  },
  "data": {
    "Version": "0.1.5",
    "CliAgentSubCohorts": [4],
    "DesktopAgentSubCohorts": [0],
    "FlushedFromSave": true
  }
}
```

JSON

I checked this with a clean installation of Windows 11 Home ARM64 using the latest official ISO, with the region set to the United States. Before changing any privacy settings, the **Diagnostic data** toggle was already enabled and labeled **Include Optional**. After completing setup with those defaults, `AllowTelemetry` was `3`, confirming that optional diagnostic data was enabled.

Optional diagnostic data is therefore enabled by default, at least in the US setup I tested. If you did not opt out of it during installation or disable optional diagnostic data later, it is still enabled and your coding agent usage data is being uploaded. You can decline optional diagnostics during setup or turn off **Send optional diagnostic data** later under **Settings → Privacy & security → Diagnostic

articles.content:
Title: “…and the proof is checked in Lean”

URL Source: https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/11/12/and-the-proof-is-checked-in-lean/

Published Time: 2026-11-12T00:50:07+00:00

Markdown Content:
This post is an attempt to explain in simple terms how to interpret claims of the form “this theorem is correct because it was checked in Lean”. The summary is: there is an important signal that can be extracted from Lean code, but if this code is AI-generated then you need to do some tests first. We explain the tests, and note that in many cases (such as the OpenAI theorem dump) these tests have not yet been systematically done.

## Introduction

Last month’s [theorem dump by OpenAI](https://github.com/openai/math) consisted of 722 mathematics papers, around 45% of which came with some Lean code. Three of the (non-Leanified) papers have since been retracted because of a sign error. Some people might say “well, the papers that come with Lean code are definitely correct because that’s how Lean works”. Others might say “well Lean had a [soundness bug](https://leodemoura.github.io/blog/2026-8-1-postmortem-for-kernel-soundness-bug-14576/) and could well have more, and AIs will reward hack, so Lean verification doesn’t tell us much at all”. The truth, unsurprisingly, is more subtle, and this post is an attempt to explain it.

This post is structured as a sequence of four questions that one needs to ask about a Lean repository, particularly if it is AI-generated, before one can start to make correctness claims of this form. And before I start, let me stress that for many of the papers in the OpenAI theorem dump, these questions have not yet all been answered affirmatively (but there is nothing stopping people from answering these questions, and I have no reason to believe that any of the tests below will fail, it’s just that people didn’t do them yet).

## Question 1. Does the Lean statement match the informal statement?

A Lean repository will typically have a “headline theorem statement”. This will be some computer code which defines the _statement_ (not the proof!) of a theorem. Note the huge difference here between the statement, and the proof. For example here is some fully-compiling Lean code which defines a mathematical statement.

This code imports Lean’s mathematics library `Mathlib` and then defines a mathematical statement which looks at first glance like it might be Fermat’s Last Theorem, but which actually is a trivially false statement because in Lean `ℕ` contains `0`, so `a = b = c = 0` and `n = 3` gives a counterexample. This does not stop the statement from compiling! It will however stop any _proof_ of this statement from compiling. Lean carefully distinguishes between the statement of a theorem and the proof of a theorem; humans are very good at referring to both ideas as “a theorem”.

The first question which one has to ask when judging a pdf which comes with some Lean code is: “what is the _statement_ of the theorem in the Lean code, and does this correspond to the actual theorem statement in the pdf?” For a human Lean expert, this is typically (but not always) an easy question to answer. For example any Lean-competent human mathematician would be able to read the two lines of code above and observe that this was a mis-statement of Fermat’s Last Theorem.

Things are, however, not always as easy as this. Currently, because of deficiencies in available libraries, one may have to read many thousands of lines of code just to understand the _statement_ of a formalised theorem. An example of this right now is a [PR to DeepMind’s Formal Conjectures repository](https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/5538) containing a Lean formalisation of the statement of the Hodge conjecture. At the time of writing, the statement relies on over 10,000 lines of code sitting on top of `Mathlib`, because `Mathlib` (which is carefully human-expert-checked and which can be trusted) does not yet have the definitions of things like the cycle class map needed to make the statement. Another example is [Axiom’s recent announcement of a formally-verified proof of the classification of finite simple groups](https://axiommath.ai/research/the-enormous-theorem-formalized/). The statement which Axiom’s system proved is [here](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/ff97e2dafb29b508b1229a5a7acbbca81ebcf3a1/TauCeti/GroupTheory/SpecificGroups/CFSG/Classification.lean#L52-L56) in Tau Ceti, an AI-generated library of Lean code. The file containing the statement imports over 250K lines of Lean code in Tau Ceti (over 900 files). Of these, around 5600 lines of code are crucial because they contain all the relevant definitions (for example, all the definitions of the sporadic simple groups, most of which are still not in `Mathlib`). Without human checking, one does not really know for sure that this is definitely the correct statement of the classification (and note that I have not yet met any human who claims to have carefully checked that the definitions of the sporadic groups in Tau Ceti are correct). In fact by far the strongest evidence that we have that this statement is correctly formalized is that Axiom’s code proves it!

It is worth noting that of the 290 OpenAI theorems which come with Lean code, around 38 of them have the property that the Lean code **does not even state, let alone prove, the main theorem of the paper**. And OpenAI never claimed that it did! They just said “here is some Lean code which goes with this paper”. Sometimes the code just states and proves some intermediate results — my impression is that OpenAI decided to go live when some of the formalizations were incomplete, so just dumped what they had. To give a concrete example: [paper 194](https://www.emergentmind.com/openai-math-explorer/results/194) claims to prove Lech’s multiplicity conjecture in commutative algebra, with no restriction on dimension, residue field or characteristic; this question has been open since 1960. The headline theorem in [the corresponding Lean code](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/lean/ComparatorChallenges/DuttaDomain.lean) can be checked to be Corollary 5.4 of the paper — already an impressive achievement, but not the headline result.

## Question 2: does the code compile?

Once you’re convinced that you understand the statement of the theorem which the Lean code purports to prove, you (or perhaps one of your friends who has access to a beefy machine, if the code base is huge) has to actually compile the code.

When Anthropic [formalized a proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in Lean](https://www.anthropic.com/research/formalizing-fermats-last-theorem), they asked me to take a look at the 13 million lines of code which they had generated. I downloaded it onto my machine, dumped it into a sandbox (because who knows what AI-generated code will do, it can in theory delete all your files) and attempted to compile it; I very quickly ran out of memory. I told Anthropic that I was unable to make any claims about what they had done until I could see the code base compiling, and they gave me temporary access to a machine with 96 cores and 500 gigs of ram. I could then compile the code.

Of course, with a more reasonably-sized codebase it is possible to compile the code on a reasonably-sized machine. For example OpenAI’s resolution of the Navier-Stokes problem is 640K lines of code and compiles fine on my laptop.

It is probably worth stressing again: do not run random Lean code on your local machine unless you sandbox it first. Lean’s mathematics library is safe to run and build upon because this is human-curated and checked by human experts. AI-generated code is not.

## Question 3: does the code prove the theorem as stated?

I already talked in Question 1 about the importance of checking the statement of a theorem, so we can be sure that the code is proving the right thing. However, there is an added complication here. Ideally the _statement_ of a theorem will be contained in a file which has very few imports beyond `Mathlib`, so we know we can trust it. But the _proof_ of the theorem will necessarily import thousands and possibly millions of lines of code which nobody wants to read. How do we know for sure that there is no trick hidden in the millions of lines of proof files which _redefines_`x^n` to mean `37`, and then proves that `a^n + b^n ≠ c^n` because the left hand side is `37+37=74` and the right hand side is `37`? Or which adds a new axiom to mathematics saying that the theorem is true? Put another way — given a `Challenge.lean` file with only trusted code imported and the statement of a theorem, and a `Solution.lean` file with millions of lines of untrusted code imported and the proof of a theorem which _looks identical_, how do we know for sure that somewhere in the millions of lines of code there is no hack which changes the _meaning_ of the statement, changes the rules from just the axioms of mathematics,

The one-line answer: `lake comparator`. You can read more about this answer [here](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/ValidatingProofs/#validating-comparator). But in short, this tool checks that the theorem stated in a trusted file and the theorem proved via untrusted imports are identical, and that only the axioms of mathematics are used in the proof.

## Question 4: does the code exploit a bug in Lean’s official kernel?

This can happen. There was a soundness bug in Lean’s kernel which was fixed four hours after it was discovered, and a subsequent review of Lean’s code base by OpenAI found several more, all of which were fixed before they were announced publicly. There may in theory be more soundness bugs in Lean’s kernel. However, _this does not matter_.

Why not? Because Lean now has many kernels, created by users, written in many different languages, and at least one of which is formally verified to have no bugs, right down to the assembly level. If you want to make absolutely sure that there is no reward-hacking then again there is a one-line answer: `lake comparator --paranoid`. A malicious piece of code exploiting an as-yet-undiscovered bug in Lean’s official kernel will not pass this test unless it exploits as-yet-undiscovered bugs in many independent systems all at once. For example [this webpage](https://arena.lean-lang.org/test/navier-stokes-euler/) from the Lean kernel arena demonstrates that OpenAI’s resolution of the Navier–Stokes problem is accepted by multiple kernels as well as Lean’s official kernel.

## One final remark

Even if the Lean code compiles and passes all these tests, and is thus overwhelmingly likely to be a correct proof of a theorem, this does not mean that any corresponding pdf also contains a correct proof! The [Navier–Stokes lost in translation paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08144) demonstrates the opposite in fact, for the Navier-Stokes write-up; whilst all the tests above have been run for the Navier–Stokes work, there are instances where the pdf proof and the Lean proof diverge. In these cases, who knows if the pdf proof is OK! My understanding is that some experts have been using AI to informalise the Lean proof back into English in order to read the argument, rather than ploughing through the slop in the pdf.

## Summary/conclusions

“It’s true because it’s checked in Lean” can be made to make sense. But one has to do some work beyond “the Lean code compiles”. Your frontier AI model can do all of this work. But it needs to be done, and (depending on the amount of Lean code in the proof) it may be computationally costly.

Title: Microsoft blames monster email outage on software defect introduced in July fix

URL Source: https://www.theregister.com/saas/2026/11/16/microsoft-blames-monster-email-outage-on-software-defect-introduced-in-july-fix/5310026

Published Time: 2026-11-16T11:15:07.000Z

Markdown Content:
REG AD

Summer code change caused a Fall fail – frantic engineers had to patch the patch instead of rolling back

Microsoft has blamed last week's [epic outage](https://www.theregister.com/saas/2026/11/13/microsoft-services-restored-to-all-customers-company-says-its-deeply-sorry/5309609) on a change it made in July that lurked in the network gateway servers until a surge in load and a drop in capacity triggered the defect, giving the Microsoft 365 world a day off from email.

According to a preliminary post incident report [published](https://x.com/clamanna/status/2122209697226948729) by Microsoft on November 15, the defect was introduced in July 2026. The update looked fine at the time, Microsoft says, having passed load testing and been deployed without any impact.

However, the testing wasn't good enough. Microsoft's report states: "Our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores." The defect caused "lock contention inside an internal Windows process which caused the machine's resources (CPU & memory) to be exhausted."

REG AD

"The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware."

REG AD

The fix containing the defect was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 network gateway servers. Then two things happened at once. Teams failed over to the"primary" gateway that supports Exchange Online, creating a surge in load that was not, in itself, particularly unusual. At the same time,almost 14 percent of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service, which wasn't a problem by itself either: it was on its way to being restored and, according to Microsoft, "the service had sufficient capacity headroom." Together, they pushed the gateway into the defect and chaos ensued.

It was a classic cascading failure scenario. When a server loses connectivity, traffic gets routed to the next healthy endpoint. Which encountered the same problem. So traffic was rerouted again and… you can see where this was going. Within two hours, the defect was encountered across Microsoft's fleet. "At its lowest," the report states, "more than 80 percent of servers were unresponsive."

So, what to do? Bringing servers back to service didn't help – they were immediately overwhelmed and fell over again.

"Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state." A straightforward rollback was also not possible because the defect was months old.

Instead, engineers developed patch for the patch or, in Microsoft's words, "an update that returned the code path to the previously known good state in Windows." The patch was applied to groups of servers and service was gradually restored.

The timings show the pain customers experienced and the floundering in Redmond as Microsoft tried to work out why Exchange Online and other cloud services were so poorly. The Teams failover, which turned out to be a factor in the outage, happened at 0107 UTC on November 12. During the day, the load began to ramp up until, at 1603 UTC, Microsoft's connectivity anomaly detection monitor identified an increase in connectivity issues.

At 1633 UTC, the first support case came in.

It is not difficult to imagine the stress engineers felt as, over the next 15 hours, nothing they tried resolved the issue. All ongoing and planned deployments and configuration changes were paused while the team attempted to resurrect the service. Extra capacity was added. Traffic was rerouted. Yet servers kept falling over.

REG AD

"Those services that were able – like Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Office apps – failed out of the faulty network gateway infrastructure," the report says."But not all services, like Exchange Online, can fail out of this network gateway for scale reasons."

Hence the length of time for which Exchange Online (or, from the perspective of many users, Outlook) was out of action.

By 0030 UTC on November 13, Microsoft had identified connection negotiation as the main culprit for the access failures and concluded that competing processes were preventing connections from being handled.

However, it took until 0720 UTC before "We identified a mitigation and applied the mitigation – an update that reverted the defective change."

At 1610 UTC, Microsoft confirmed that things were once again looking healthy and, at 0415 on November 14, issued its final customer update.

A final post incident report is due on November 20. However, the preliminary report will do little to calm jangling nerves. An update applied three months ago managed to cause Exchange Online (and other services) disruption on a global scale? With load testing that didn't reflect scenarios under Microsoft's control?

The engineers who worked feverishly to restore services deserve commendation and will hopefully never have to buy their own beverages in Redmond again (or at least escape the next round of firings). However, the processes that led to an update with a latent defect reaching production deserve a long, hard look. ®

Pilot announces systems are back online after United Airlines widespread system outage

A widespread, yet short-lived, system outage at United Airlines on Monday delayed some outbound flights at US airports, the airline told CNN in a statement, coming on the heels of a [rare FAA ground stop](https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/14/politics/faa-ground-stop-what-we-know) that caused [massive disruption](https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/13/us/live-news/flights-ground-stop-faa).

The outage lasted about 30 minutes, with fewer than 150 flights impacted, United Airlines spokesperson Leslie Scott told CNN.

United [acknowledged](https://x.com/united/status/2122449364819886277) the issue just before 5 p.m. ET, saying the technology outage was impacting departing flights, and an hour later the airline announced it had been resolved.

Ad Feedback

“While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights,” United Airlines said in a statement.

During the incident, the FAA said United was experiencing a technology outage on its end and that “it’s not an FAA equipment issue.”

[Related article  CNN ‘Working on floppy disks’: FAA has fielded years of warnings about old systems 7 min read](https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/16/us/faa-ground-stop-warnings-invs)

United said there is no indication that the outage was a cybersecurity-related issue.

The technology outage affected access to multiple applications used by flight crews, according to an internal company alert obtained by CNN.

The airline instructed pilots not to log out of several systems, warning they may be unable to sign back in. The affected applications included flight planning, weather briefing and crew management tools.

Pilots unable to access their flight plans were being directed to contact dispatchers to have the documents emailed to them.

The memo did not disclose the cause of the outage.

Air traffic control audio captured by [ATC.com](http://atc.com/) shows the moment the outage occurred.

“Hey, we’re uh, still waiting on our final weights,” a pilot on United Flight 1728 in El Paso, heading to Denver, said to a controller. “We just contacted ops and apparently there’s a company-wide system outage on it so might be a while.”

The controller responds back, “United 1728, roger, so you don’t have any idea when you think you’ll be able to leave?”

“No ma’am,” the pilot responds.

## Aviation industry still recovering from weekend ground stop

The industry had largely returned to normal operations after the nationwide ground stop was lifted just after 8 p.m. ET on Friday, though airlines have still worked to reposition [planes, crews and luggage](https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/14/us/live-news/us-ground-stop-flights?post-id=cmwgq5lyx00003b6utawcyem5) as they grappled with the weekend’s [score of cancellations and delays](https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/14/us/live-news/us-ground-stop-flights?post-id=cmwgqcoig0000356vzunestfq).

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy held a 45-minute news conference Saturday morning to address the FAA ground stop, and apologized to travelers as he said he was still working to determine what exactly went wrong.

[Related article  A traveler waits in line at John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York on November 14. Ryan Murphy/Getty Images With the busiest travel season ahead, how likely is it that another FAA ground stop happens? 8 min read](https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/16/us/faa-ground-stop-thanksgiving-travel)

Duffy told reporters that [upgrade work on an old telecommunication system](https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/14/politics/faa-ground-stop-what-we-know) could be a cause for Friday’s nationwide ground stop.

In at least one remote FAA location, Duffy said contractor L3Harris was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from an old copper wire to fiber, which he described as “straightforward” work that has been happening across the country for decades.

As United Airlines indicated for Monday’s system outage, Friday’s ground stop didn’t appear to have been caused by a cyber attack or any “nefarious” activity, Duffy stressed at the news conference.

“A lot of questions came in yesterday. ‘Was this a, a cyber attack? Did some foreign nation attack this network?’ And the answer to that is we don’t believe so,” Duffy said.

# Spamhaus Sender Guidelines

Requirements and recommendations to help email senders follow best practices and strengthen trust and safety on the internet.

 Sections

HELO/DNS checker

1. Infrastructure and DNS Reverse DNS (rDNS)HELO/EHLO IP space and routing From domain (Envelope FROM)DNS hygiene

2. Authentication SPF (Sender Policy Framework)DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail)DMARC

3. Permission and List Hygiene Permission Spamtraps

4. Sending best practices Warm up Bounce management Unsubscribe Content

5. IP and Domain Reputation

6. ESPs & Large Senders

Tools & Resources

Note

Starting in **November 2026**, we are gradually rolling out a requirement for every sending IP to have a valid HELO, a reverse DNS (PTR) record, and a matching A record. Use the HELO checker below to see whether the DNS meets our best practices, and follow the guidelines to avoid being listed.

Minimum requirements

Guidance for senders, mail admins, and postmasters on meeting Spamhaus's sending requirements. All senders must meet these minimum email sending requirements to avoid being listed.

1.   1 Use confirmed opt-in (COI) for all subscribers

Each recipient should confirm their address by clicking a link in a confirmation email. If no confirmation is received, do not send email to that address. Purchased, rented and harvested lists are the most common source of spam trap hits, and hitting traps is one of the fastest routes to a listing.[See section](https://www.spamhaus.org/sender-guidelines/#3-permission-and-list-hygiene--permission)
2.   2 Publish forward-confirmed reverse DNS for every sending IP

Every sending IP must have a reverse DNS entry pointing to a fully qualified domain name (FQDN). That hostname must, in turn, resolve back to the same sending IP address. This is known as forward-confirmed reverse DNS (FCrDNS). An IP with missing or mismatched reverse DNS is treated as suspicious and is one of the most common reasons for an IP to be considered for listing.[See section](https://www.spamhaus.org/sender-guidelines/#1-infrastructure-and-dns--reverse-dns-rdns)
3.   3 Use a HELO/EHLO hostname that resolves to the sending IP

The hostname the server announces in the HELO/EHLO command must resolve to the IP it is connecting from, and must stay consistent across connections from that IP. Placeholder values, hosting-provider defaults, and hostnames that vary between connections are treated as signals of misconfiguration or compromise and can result in a listing.[See section](https://www.spamhaus.org/sender-guidelines/#1-infrastructure-and-dns--helo-ehlo)
4.   4 Meet the IPv6 allocation and reverse DNS minimum

If sending over IPv6, the sending address must fall within an allocation of /64 or larger (a /64 is the standard block size we recommend assigning), and that space must have valid reverse DNS. IPv6 ranges without reverse DNS or with allocations smaller than /64 are often misused by spammers.[See section](https://www.spamhaus.org/sender-guidelines/#1-infrastructure-and-dns--ip-space-and-routing)
5.   5 Authenticate mail with [SPF](https://www.spamhaus.org/glossary/#spf-sender-policy-framework), [DKIM](https://www.spamhaus.org/glossary/#dkim-domainkeys-identified-mail) and [DMARC](https://www.spamhaus.org/glossary/#dmarc-domain-based-message-authentication-reporting-and-conformance)

Publish SPF and DMARC records for every sending domain, sign every outbound message with a signature, and align the DKIM sending domain with the domain in the message's [RFC 5322](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc5322/) From address. Authentication is one of the signals that shapes reputation, so gaps here make a listing more likely when other signals are weak.[See section](https://www.spamhaus.org/sender-guidelines/#2-authentication)

[Operating an Email Server Provider (ESP) or other shared sending infrastructure? **See the ESPs and Large Senders guidelines**](https://www.spamhaus.org/sender-guidelines/esp-large-senders/)

Check your HELO and DNS setup

Enter your sending IP to check its HELO and DNS setup against our guidelines. Results may not be available for all IPs and some queries might not provide results for internal policy reasons. You can also check the current HELO by sending an email to [helocheck@abuseat.org](mailto:helocheck@abuseat.org).

Check HELO/DNS

## 1. Infrastructure and DNS

All sending infrastructure must have the following DNS and mailserver configuration. Failure to do so can result in IPs being listed on the Email Spam IPs (CSS) or compromised IPs (XBL) zones.

Collapse all

Reverse DNS (rDNS)

Do

Don't

Do

 Required

*   Ensure the sending IP address has a valid **reverse DNS (rDNS)** entry resolving to a fully qualified domain name (FQDN) for the sending IP address. Spamhaus will treat emails originating from IP addresses without rDNS as suspicious and this will be reflected in the IP's reputation, and receivers using Spamhaus data may subject it to additional filtering.
*   Ensure the rDNS hostname resolves to the connecting IP address via a corresponding **forward DNS (A/AAAA) record**.

 Recommended

*   Abusive actors often rely on the reputation of upstream DNS records to hide their identity. Instead, configure a branded reverse DNS to use the sender's own domain, to improve trust signals for the IP address.

Don't

*   Do not use generic or auto-generated rDNS entries for dedicated IPs that point to the hosting provider (e.g., `static-203-0-113-25.hosting.example.net`, `203.113.0.25.broadband.example.net`, `vps-25.dedicated.hosting.example.com` etc). These can negatively impact reputation.
*   Do not use random dictionary words in the rDNS and make it identifiable to the sending infrastructure.

How to check

Use the [Spamhaus DNS checker](https://www.spamhaus.org/sender-guidelines/#dns-checker) tool to check your rDNS configuration.

HELO/EHLO

Do

Don't

Do

 Required

*   Ensure the hostname used in the **HELO/EHLO** command resolves to the sending IP address.
*   Maintain a consistent HELO value that resolves to the sending IP address. Multiple HELO values resolving to different IP addresses may indicate residential proxy and/or malware behaviour.

 Recommended

*   Where possible, ensure the HELO/EHLO hostname is consistent with the rDNS hostname.
*   Host a webpage on the domain of the HELO, that explains what the domain is for, or that redirects to the main brand domain.

Don't

*   Do not use placeholder values such as `localhost` or generic hostnames that point to the hosting company/ISP as the HELO value.
*   Do not resolve HELO hostname to infrastructure that is not used for sending — this behaviour is associated with spoofing and misconfiguration.
*   Do not use generic or auto-generated names provided by the hosting provider, use the sender's own domain where possible.
*   Do not impersonate the HELO value of well-known mailbox providers like Gmail or Hotmail.

How to check

Enter an IP address into the [Spamhaus DNS Checker at the top of this page](https://www.spamhaus.org/sender-guidelines/#dns-checker), to check its HELO value. An email can also be sent to [helocheck@abuseat.org](mailto:helocheck@abuseat.org) to check the HELO being used.

IP space and routing

Do

Do

 Required

*   IPv6 customer allocations must be at least /64 and must have valid reverse DNS. The /64 minimum is consistent with IPv6 subnet architecture and [RFC 6177](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc6177/)'s guidance that email senders should be able to obtain at least a /64. This is further discussed in [M3AAWG best practices](https://www.m3aawg.org/sites/default/files/document/M3AAWG_Inbound_IPv6_Policy_Issues-2014-09.pdf) for IPv6 allocation.

 Recommended

*   Add routes for all IP space owned by the sender to reduce vulnerability to [BGP hijacking](https://www.spamhaus.org/resource-hub/network-security/fighting-abuse-at-the-edge/#how-do-bad-guys-acquire-control-of-ip-address-ranges), which can allow hackers to send email that appears to originate from the IP space.

How to check

Run `dig -x <an IPv6 address in the allocation>` to confirm reverse DNS is present. To confirm the space is actually routed, look the address up at [bgp.he.net](https://bgp.he.net/).

From domain (Envelope FROM)

Do

Don't

Do

 Required

*   Make sure SPF is set up correctly for the domain used in the envelope sender ([RFC 5321](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc5321/) MAIL FROM), and points to the sending infrastructure.
*   Use [SRS](http://www.open-spf.org/SRS/) (Sender Rewriting Scheme) to rewrite the envelope From (MAIL FROM) if mail is forwarded, so SPF can still be checked against the forwarding domain.

Don't

*   Do not allow freemail addresses such as `gmail.com` or `hotmail.com` as the 'Envelope FROM.'
*   Do not use the NULL envelope sender `<>` for anything other than indirect out-of-band delivery reports, DSNs and MDNs.
*   Do not send bounce messages after accepting unwanted mail. Reject it during the SMTP transaction instead. Bounces sent to forged senders are known as backscatter, which is indirect spam and can severely harm reputation.

How to check

Run `dig TXT <envelope sender domain>` and confirm an SPF record is returned and includes the sending IPs.

DNS hygiene

Do

Don't

Do

 Recommended

*   Audit DNS regularly and remove records for services, hosts and IP space that are no longer used, including [CNAMEs](https://www.spamhaus.org/glossary/#cname-record), NS delegations, A records and SPF `include:` entries for former providers.

Don't

*   Do not leave records pointing to decommissioned hosts or former providers. [Dangling records](https://www.spamhaus.org/resource-hub/dns/dangling-dns-and-the-dangers-of-subdomain-hijacking/) can be claimed by others and used to send mail that appears to come from the domain.
*   Do not use wildcard DNS records.

This [article](https://www.wordtothewise.com/2024/07/sending-domains-and-hostnames/) explains domain, hostname terminology and domain alignment in email. Also, use [aboutmy.email](https://aboutmy.email/) to check for email configuration setup.

How to check

Run `dig` against the subdomains and look for CNAMEs that resolve to a provider that no longer serves the domain.

Title: Running coding agents without handing them my credentials

URL Source: https://blog.antonio.cx/running-agents-with-lend

Markdown Content:
2026-11-13·[antonio's blog](https://blog.antonio.cx/)

* * *

## Table of Contents

    *   [Keeping the socket stable across reconnects](https://blog.antonio.cx/running-agents-with-lend#keeping-the-socket-stable-across-reconnects)

> I built [lend](https://github.com/antoniomika/lend) to let remote agents use tools on my laptop with my approval. Here's how it fits into my workflow.

## Background [#](https://blog.antonio.cx/running-agents-with-lend#background)

I use agents heavily these days as part of my toolchain. I usually have a few going at once: Claude Code working in one repo, Codex reviewing a branch in another, and something long-running in the background. I often have them review each other's work too. None of them run on my laptop. They run on VMs I can throw away, and my laptop keeps the stuff I care about: my SSH keys, my 1Password vault, and the `gh` and cloud CLIs that are logged in as me.

I run those agents on [picd](https://cd.pico.sh/), our hosting service at [pico.sh](https://pico.sh/). It gives me my own VM with a Docker engine and a shell over SSH. I run herdr and the agents there, and my home directory persists across restarts so my dotfiles and tools stay in place.

This works great until an agent needs something on my laptop. In this post I'll go over how I run agents in parallel with [herdr](https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr) and [Ovis](https://ovis.sh/), and the tool I wrote to deal with credentials, [lend](https://lend.antonio.cx/).

## herdr [#](https://blog.antonio.cx/running-agents-with-lend#herdr)

herdr is a terminal multiplexer built for coding agents. You get the usual workspaces, tabs, and panes, and it also knows which agent is running in each pane and what it's doing. The sidebar shows whether each agent is working, waiting on me, or done, so I can tell at a glance which one needs attention.

The CLI talks to the running session, so agents can drive each other. An agent can start Codex in another pane, give it a prompt, wait for it to finish, and read what it said:

```
1herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane "$PANE"
2herdr agent prompt reviewer "Review the diff on am/fix-retries" --wait --until done
3herdr agent read reviewer --source recent
```

Remote hosts work the same way. `herdr machine add agent-vm` sets up herdr on the VM and adds its sessions to my local client. Those sessions keep running after I disconnect.

## Ovis [#](https://blog.antonio.cx/running-agents-with-lend#ovis)

Ovis is a browser and phone client for herdr. It shows each agent's transcript as a chat, with the live terminal a tap away. When an agent asks for approval or has a question, Ovis turns it into a card I can answer and sends me a push notification. It picks up the machines saved in herdr, so my VMs show up without any extra setup. I reach it over Tailscale.

If an agent gets stuck on a question while I'm away from my desk, I answer it from my phone and the other agents keep going.

## The credential problem [#](https://blog.antonio.cx/running-agents-with-lend#the-credential-problem)

Agents on a VM still need to act as me. I use them to monitor CI with `gh`, call APIs with tokens from 1Password, and SSH into other hosts. There are two usual ways to make that work, and I don't love either of them.

The first is copying credentials onto the VM. A token in `~/.config/gh/hosts.yml` can be read by every process on that machine, including the agent and anything it runs, for as long as the token is valid.

The second is forwarding my SSH agent with `ssh -A`. The private keys stay on my laptop, but the VM can use every key in the agent without asking and without any record of what it signed. It also only covers SSH keys.

What I wanted was for the credentials to stay on the laptop and for the commands that need them to run there too. The agent asks to run something, I approve it with Touch ID, and the agent gets the output back.

## lend [#](https://blog.antonio.cx/running-agents-with-lend#lend)

That's where lend comes in. lend is a proxy that sits in front of your existing SSH agent, and you forward its socket in place of the real one. SSH and Git keep working like normal, and lend adds a way to run commands through an SSH agent extension.

When an agent on the VM asks to run `gh`, the request goes over the socket and `gh` runs on my laptop with my login. The token never leaves the laptop, so the agent never has it. Every request, whether it's a signature or a command, is checked against a policy on the laptop and needs my approval before anything happens.

```
1Remote: lend exec -- command args
2                  |
3          forwarded SSH agent socket
4                  |
5Laptop: lend agent -> policy + local approval -> local command
6                                           -> original SSH agent (signing)
```

The policy lives on the laptop and lists what the VM is allowed to ask for. Everything else is denied. Mine is pretty short:

```
1{
 2  "default": "deny",
 3  "commands": [
 4    {"executable": "/opt/homebrew/bin/gh", "approval": "biometric:inline"}
 5  ],
 6  "ssh": {
 7    "default": "deny",
 8    "keys": [
 9      {"fingerprint": "SHA256:...", "approval": "biometric:inline"}
10    ]
11  }
12}
```

A rule can also take an `args_prefix` like `["pr", "view"]` if you only want to allow some subcommands. `biometric:inline` puts Touch ID right in the request dialog, so I read the request and touch once to approve it. Plain `biometric` asks for Touch ID in a second prompt after I click Allow.

To connect, I run `lend ssh` from the laptop. It starts a proxy for that one connection and stops it when SSH exits:

```
1lend ssh --config ./policy.json -- agent-vm
```

I run herdr on the VM. Claude Code talks to lend through `lend mcp`, an MCP server with a single tool called `run_local_command`. The tool takes the command to run and a reason, and the reason is required:

```
1{
2  "mcpServers": {
3    "laptop": {"command": "lend", "args": ["mcp"]}
4  }
5}
```

Here I asked Claude Code on the VM for the lend repo's description. It called the tool with `gh repo view`, my Mac showed the request, and one touch approved it:

The dialog shows the full path to the executable, every argument, the directory it'll run in on the laptop, the reason, and what the remote process said about itself. Once I approve, `gh` runs on the laptop and stdout, stderr, and the exit code stream back to the agent. The reason and caller details come from the VM, so they're marked as unverified. They're there to help me decide and can't change what the policy allows.

If you'd rather skip MCP, the same request works as a plain CLI call on the VM:

```
1lend exec --reason "Read the repo description" -- gh repo view antoniomika/lend
```

### Keeping the socket stable across reconnects [#](https://blog.antonio.cx/running-agents-with-lend#keeping-the-socket-stable-across-reconnects)

herdr panes survive an SSH disconnect, but the forwarded socket belongs to that connection. When I reconnect, SSH gives me a new socket path. Agents still running in the panes keep the old `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`.

I use a symlink at a fixed path and update it from [`~/.ssh/rc`](https://man.openbsd.org/sshd.8#SSHRC) on the VM. SSH runs this before starting the shell, so it sees the socket forwarded by the new connection:

```
1#!/bin/sh
 2
 3if [ -n "${SSH_AUTH_SOCK:-}" ] &&
 4    [ "$SSH_AUTH_SOCK" != "$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock" ] &&
 5    "$HOME/.local/bin/lend" doctor --remote --socket "$SSH_AUTH_SOCK" --timeout 1s >/dev/null 2>&1; then
 6  install -d -m 700 "$HOME/.ssh/lend" &&
 7    ln -sfn -- "$SSH_AUTH_SOCK" "$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock"
 8fi
 9
10if [ -n "${DISPLAY:-}" ] && read -r _ssh_proto _ssh_cookie; then
11  case $DISPLAY in
12    localhost:*) _ssh_display="unix:${DISPLAY#localhost:}" ;;
13    *) _ssh_display=$DISPLAY ;;
14  esac
15  printf 'add %s %s %s\n' "$_ssh_display" "$_ssh_proto" "$_ssh_cookie" | /usr/bin/xauth -q -
16fi
```

The check confirms the forwarded socket speaks lend before updating the link. The directory is private to my user and keeps this link separate from other agent sockets. I use lend's absolute path because this runs before my shell adds `~/.local/bin` to `PATH`. The X11 block handles cookie setup, which SSH delegates to this file when it exists.

My `~/.bashrc` checks the stable path before exporting it:

```
1if [ -S "$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock" ] &&
2    "$HOME/.local/bin/lend" doctor --remote --socket "$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock" --timeout 1s >/dev/null 2>&1; then
3  export SSH_AUTH_SOCK="$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock"
4fi
```

New Bash shells in herdr panes pick up the stable path when it works. If the check fails, Bash leaves `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` alone. MCP, approval hooks, and Git inherit that path when I start them. After reconnecting, the SSH hook updates the symlink and those processes use the new socket for subsequent requests. Agents already running with an old socket path need to be restarted once with the stable path in their environment.

The SSH connection from the laptop still has to stay open. Requests fail while it's disconnected, and reconnecting starts a new lend session with fresh approvals and leases. The link points at one connection at a time, so the last update wins.

### Secrets the agent never sees [#](https://blog.antonio.cx/running-agents-with-lend#secrets-the-agent-never-sees)

`gh` works because it's already logged in on my laptop. Some tools need a token passed in. For those, a command rule can read secrets with something like `op read` and hand them to the approved command as environment variables:

```
1{
 2  "secret_reader": "/opt/homebrew/bin/op",
 3  "secret_reader_args": ["read", "--no-newline"],
 4  "commands": [
 5    {
 6      "executable": "/opt/homebrew/bin/gh",
 7      "args_prefix": ["pr", "view"],
 8      "approval": "biometric",
 9      "secrets": {"GH_TOKEN": "op://Development/github/token"}
10    }
11  ]
12}
```

When the agent asks to run `gh pr view` and I approve it, lend reads the token from 1Password, runs `gh` with `GH_TOKEN` set, and sends back the output. The token stays on the laptop. The VM can't pick which variables get set or which references get read. The prompt shows the variable names and references, and the values never show up in prompts or history.

Here's the VM running `gh api user` with a rule that injects `GH_TOKEN`. After I approve in lend, 1Password asks for its own Touch ID before `op read` returns the token. The VM gets my login back, and its own environment has no `GH_TOKEN`:

There's one catch: this only works if the approved command doesn't print its environment. If you approve `env` or `sh`, you've handed the values right back. The same goes for allowing `op` itself as a command, since `op read` prints the secret and that output goes straight to the agent.

### SSH keys [#](https://blog.antonio.cx/running-agents-with-lend#ssh-keys)

Keys get their own policy too. Keys that aren't listed are hidden from the VM, and listed keys can be limited by what they're allowed to sign. `max_signatures` caps how many signatures a key can make in a session.

### Leases [#](https://blog.antonio.cx/running-agents-with-lend#leases)

A rule can offer a lease when I approve, like five minutes or three uses. Leases only exist inside a `lend ssh` session and only match the exact command and arguments I approved. They go away when the session ends or my screen locks.

### Seeing what happened [#](https://blog.antonio.cx/running-agents-with-lend#seeing-what-happened)

`lend status --all --watch` shows what's connected, what's waiting, what's running, and any active leases. `lend pause --all` cancels everything and refuses new requests until I resume. `lend history` keeps a record of what ran and how it was approved. Anthropic told IPO investors that its Claude Mythos Preview model did the software work required to get its AI running on AMD’s GPUs in about three days, with “basically no human intervention,” a job it says used to take six to 12 months. The three days cover prompt processing for one Anthropic model on AMD MI355X GPUs “at a useful level of performance,” with Mythos porting or writing “almost 100% of the kernels.” That kind of low-level code, which ties an AI model to one company’s chips, has long been part of Nvidia’s CUDA moat, and an AI that can write it in days would suggest that moat is eroding.
Tom Brown, Anthropic’s co-founder and chief compute officer, made the time comparison, noting
to investors
that the original meant using a team of “dozens of engineers.” The company already runs its models on multiple kinds of chips — on GPUs from Nvidia and AMD,
Google
’s TPUs, and AWS Trainium — and its fleet is managed as “one fungible pool of compute.” Brown called the early multi-chip decision “an unconventional bet.” It may have been a wise one, given that Google’s
TPUs can now natively run AI models built in PyTorch
, and Meta uses them in production.
Anthropic's claim that the job used to take six to 12 months comes from past work, from its “historical experience bringing up new accelerators using traditional engineering approaches,” where tailoring the code to each hardware platform was a challenge. Removing that onboarding barrier could reduce things to a purchase decision, and Anthropic started working with AMD GPUs for the first time this year, with
an agreement for up to 2 gigawatts
now in place.

CUDA, Nvidia’s programming platform, is very mature at nearly two decades old. AMD has an equivalent, ROCm, with HIP as its programming layer. Code written for CUDA has to be transformed to work there, and AMD even built a tool called HIPify for the process. There is still a conversion cost to switching, and AMD’s vice president of AI software, Anush Elangovan, told
EE Times
in April that “Claude is better than HIPify because it has web search built in.”
AMD has been making the argument that AI can write this type of code since August of last year, presenting a research agent that fell short of human experts at the time. In September of that year, AMD CEO Lisa Su said on the
Possible
podcast
that much of AI software is written in CUDA, which needs to be “translated to AMD,” and “a ton of that can now be done in software.”
Moving forward to July earlier this year, AMD’s senior vice president of AI, Vamsi Boppana, said its engineers were using AI models to generate GPU kernels, and Su said that when she asked whether her team was helping the Anthropic engineer working on the MI355X, she was told they didn’t need any help. Boppana said that in some cases, the resulting kernels were even “better than the most manually tuned versions.” Under its July agreement with Anthropic, AMD is also using Claude to optimize workloads for its Instinct GPUs and to speed up ROCm development.
At AMD’s
Advancing AI event in July
, OpenAI’s Philippe Tillet said that once OpenAI got its Helios racks, a single engineer confirmed everything worked within a few days, and that “agents are taking over our jobs, in a sense, as kernel engineers.” Before the event, AMD’s Andrew Dieckman, corporate vice president and general manager of the company’s data center GPU business, told reporters that he has had practically zero conversations with AMD’s customers about CUDA.

Until this week, though, all of this came from AMD or its stage, not from Anthropic to its own investors. Anthropic buys the chips rather than selling them, and it’s heading into
its IPO
next week, so its multi-chip approach — now with at least some numbers to back it up — carries more weight than a chipmaker’s claims. Its prospectus says it in writing, too, though without a number: “We can onboard new chip platforms in a fraction of the time it once took.”

The prompt processing (prefill) part of the workload is the step where a model reads and processes what it’s been given before it starts replying, and Anthropic hasn’t said whether the replying step (decode) was included as well. Anthropic’s chart, with its axis labeled “Time to onboard new silicon,” shows both lines reaching the same “~100%” mark without saying 100% of what. The company also hasn’t said how fast the model ran on AMD’s GPUs versus Nvidia’s, and that’s the comparison we want to see to show whether AMD’s chips, running AI-written code, can match Nvidia silicon.
(Image credit: Anthropic)
On the other hand, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in an April interview with Dwarkesh Patel that Nvidia already uses AI on its own kernels and knows its chips best — “nobody knows our architecture better than we do” — and can get the most out of them. Asked why labs like Anthropic use other accelerators, he called Anthropic “a unique instance, not a trend.” Nvidia and AMD, among seven companies, are buying $26.0 billion of Anthropic’s stock at the IPO price, so Nvidia is investing in the very company Huang called the exception.
In late July,
SemiAnalysis
published an article, “Can AMD break the CUDA Moat?,” which essentially said that software creation is not the same moat it was even a year ago. That said, the catch for AMD is that with agentic coding, “each agent requires GPUs to test their code against,” which means that the AI writing the code still needs the hardware. It has found a constant lack of GPUs inside AMD for this type of development, which has held AMD back and may be a new bottleneck.
That leaves CUDA’s moat somewhere in between. Getting a model running on a new chip, once the expensive part, appears to be getting cheaper, and better AI may wear down Nvidia’s claim that it knows its hardware best. As for Anthropic’s fungible pool, the chips in it aren’t fully interchangeable — Google’s TPUs are
increasingly specialized
, for example — and getting the most out of any of them still takes the hardware to test on. The moat is narrowing, but is not gone.
Anthropic’s first AMD MI450 chips,
in Helios racks
, are expected in the first half of 2027. That’s a new generation and an opportunity to see if the three-day bring-up can be repeated. Anthropic’s IPO comes sooner, after which it will report as a public company.
